explanation.summary: The modified Duke criteria establish definite endocarditis with 2 majors, 1 major plus 3 minors, or 5 minors. Typical organism from persistently positive blood cultures is one major; echocardiographic vegetation with new valvular regurgitation is a second. This patient meets both, warranting a definite diagnosis and immediate treatment planning with cardiology and cardiac surgery input given the prosthetic valve.
key_points: Major criteria: typical organism in 2 or more separate blood cultures; echocardiographic evidence (vegetation, abscess, new prosthetic dehiscence, new regurgitation)
Minor criteria: predisposing condition, fever above 38, vascular phenomena (splinters, Janeway), immunologic (Osler, Roth), microbiological non-major
Prosthetic valve endocarditis requires early cardiac surgery review
explanation.pearls: Splinter haemorrhages do not count as a major criterion. They are a minor vascular phenomenon. Echocardiographic vegetation is the major.

sources.label: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

options.rationale: The echocardiographic vegetation with new regurgitation on a prosthetic valve is a separate MAJOR criterion, not a minor. Two majors are present. (Source: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ)
source_refs: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

options.rationale: There are not 4 minor criteria here (fever above 38 is one minor, splinter haemorrhages are one minor); more importantly the echocardiographic evidence is major and completes a 2-major definite diagnosis. (Source: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ)
source_refs: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

options.rationale: Persistent bacteraemia with typical organism and echocardiographic vegetation are both majors, not minors. This case is diagnosed on 2 majors. (Source: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ)
source_refs: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

options.rationale: Two majors are clearly present. Cardiac MRI is an adjunct in problem cases but is not required to make the diagnosis here. (Source: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ)
source_refs: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

options.rationale: Modified Duke definite endocarditis requires either 2 majors, or 1 major plus 3 minors, or 5 minors. Here the typical organism from persistently positive blood cultures satisfies one major, and the echocardiographic vegetation plus new regurgitation satisfies the second. (Source: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ)
source_refs: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

explanation.summary: GOLD Group E (2 or more moderate exacerbations or 1 hospitalisation in the past year) requires escalation from LAMA monotherapy to LABA plus LAMA. Triple therapy is reserved for patients with continued exacerbations on dual bronchodilator AND eosinophils at or above 300. Non-pharmacological measures (pulmonary rehab, smoking cessation, vaccination) run in parallel.
key_points: Group E: 2 or more moderate exacerbations OR 1 hospitalisation in the past year
Escalate LAMA to LABA plus LAMA first; add ICS only if continued exacerbations and eosinophils at or above 300
COPD-X aligns with GOLD 2023 in Australia
explanation.pearls: Do not skip to triple therapy in a patient with only one prior hospitalisation. Dual bronchodilator is the correct next step; add ICS only if that fails and eosinophils support it.

sources.label: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

options.rationale: For GOLD Group E COPD (2 or more moderate exacerbations or 1 hospitalisation in the past year), GOLD 2023 recommends escalating from LAMA monotherapy to LABA plus LAMA. Triple therapy (LABA plus LAMA plus ICS) is added if exacerbations persist AND eosinophils are at or above 300. His eosinophil count is 320 but the initial escalation is dual bronchodilator. (Source: GOLD 2023 COPD Report; Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

options.rationale: Group E COPD requires escalation of maintenance therapy, not continuation of monotherapy. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

options.rationale: Triple therapy is indicated for Group E patients with continued exacerbations on LABA plus LAMA and eosinophils at or above 300. Jumping straight to triple therapy skips the intermediate step. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

options.rationale: Theophylline is a last-resort option due to its narrow therapeutic index and drug interactions and is not recommended before dual bronchodilator escalation. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

options.rationale: Chronic oral corticosteroid therapy is not recommended for stable COPD outside end-stage disease due to systemic toxicity without exacerbation benefit. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

explanation.summary: Reversal agents for direct oral anticoagulants are drug-specific. Andexanet alfa reverses the factor Xa inhibitors apixaban and rivaroxaban; idarucizumab reverses the direct thrombin inhibitor dabigatran. Where andexanet alfa is unavailable, 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate at 50 units/kg is used off-label. Vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma are ineffective for DOAC reversal.
key_points: Andexanet alfa for apixaban and rivaroxaban; idarucizumab for dabigatran
4-factor PCC at 50 units/kg is off-label alternative for factor Xa inhibitor reversal
Vitamin K, FFP, TXA are not effective DOAC reversal agents
explanation.pearls: Match the reversal to the DOAC mechanism. Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, not apixaban.

sources.label: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus

options.rationale: Idarucizumab is specific for the direct thrombin inhibitor dabigatran, not the factor Xa inhibitor apixaban. It has no effect on apixaban. (Source: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus)
source_refs: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus

options.rationale: Andexanet alfa is a specific reversal agent for the factor Xa inhibitors apixaban and rivaroxaban and is approved in Australia for life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding. Dosing is stratified by last dose amount and time since last dose. (Source: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus)
source_refs: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus

options.rationale: This is the AU reversal protocol for warfarin-associated bleeding, not apixaban. Vitamin K has no role in reversing DOACs. (Source: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus)
source_refs: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus

options.rationale: Fresh frozen plasma does not effectively reverse DOAC anticoagulant effect and is not recommended as first-line. (Source: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus)
source_refs: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus

options.rationale: Tranexamic acid does not reverse the DOAC anticoagulant effect. It has an emerging adjunct role but is not a specific DOAC reversal agent. (Source: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus)
source_refs: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus

explanation.summary: The Australian Sepsis Network hour-1 bundle is a fixed sequence: measure lactate, obtain cultures before antibiotics, administer broad-spectrum empirical antibiotics, commence 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4, and start vasopressors if MAP under 65 despite fluid. Source control (in this case percutaneous nephrostomy for the obstructed infected kidney) is added urgently but does not delay the bundle.
key_points: Cultures before antibiotics unless drawing cultures would delay antibiotics
30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate greater than 4
Vasopressor of choice is noradrenaline; target MAP at least 65 mmHg
Source control in obstructed pyelonephritis is percutaneous nephrostomy urgently
explanation.pearls: Empiric AU cover for community urosepsis is piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin (or ceftriaxone plus gentamicin). Adjust with cultures at 24 to 48 hours.

sources.label: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Sepsis and septic shock

options.rationale: Vasopressors are added only after fluid resuscitation has failed to restore MAP to 65 or above. Starting them first violates the bundle. (Source: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway

options.rationale: Cultures should be obtained BEFORE antibiotics whenever possible without delaying antibiotics. Fluid dose is 30 mL/kg, not 20. (Source: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway

options.rationale: Antibiotics must be given within 1 hour empirically for septic shock. Waiting for cultures increases mortality. (Source: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway

options.rationale: The Surviving Sepsis and Australian Sepsis Network hour-1 bundle is: measure lactate, obtain cultures before antibiotics, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics, commence 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4, and start vasopressors if MAP under 65 despite fluid. Urgent source control (nephrostomy) is added in obstructed pyelonephritis. (Source: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway

options.rationale: Imaging should not delay the bundle. The source is already identified on point-of-care ultrasound with confirmed obstruction and pyuria. (Source: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis in a known Addison's patient with vomiting and hypotension requires immediate parenteral hydrocortisone 100 mg IM or IV followed by 200 mg over 24 hours (or 50 mg every 6 hours). Concurrent 0.9 percent sodium chloride and dextrose correct volume, glucose, and electrolyte disturbances. Fludrocortisone is not needed acutely because high-dose hydrocortisone provides mineralocorticoid effect.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IM or IV stat, then 200 mg over 24 hours or 50 mg every 6 hours
0.9 percent saline resuscitation and 5 percent dextrose for hypoglycaemia and volume
Sick day rules: double or triple oral dose for illness; parenteral if vomiting; carry emergency kit
explanation.pearls: The single commonest cause of death in Addison's is failure to give parenteral hydrocortisone during acute illness. Never wait for confirmatory tests when the diagnosis is known.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines

options.rationale: Dexamethasone is used only when the diagnosis of primary adrenal insufficiency is not yet made and a synacthen test is planned in the next few hours. Diagnosis is already established; hydrocortisone is the correct choice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal insufficiency)

The hyperkalaemia will correct with steroid, fluid and glucose (via insulin) therapy. Deferring hydrocortisone is dangerous and inappropriate; calcium can be given for ECG changes but does not replace hydrocortisone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal insufficiency)

Oral steroid in a vomiting patient is unreliable and delays effective replacement. Parenteral hydrocortisone is required immediately. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal insufficiency)

Fludrocortisone is oral only and its mineralocorticoid effect is provided by high-dose hydrocortisone (which has intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity at 100 mg doses). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal insufficiency)

Suspected or confirmed adrenal crisis requires immediate parenteral hydrocortisone 100 mg then 200 mg over 24 hours, plus fluid and glucose resuscitation. Delay for confirmatory testing is inappropriate. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: In chronic or subacute symptomatic hyponatraemia, the correction rate ceiling is 8 mmol/L in 24 hours (6 in high-risk groups). Severe symptoms (seizures, coma) are treated with a 100 mL 3 percent saline bolus, repeated as needed until symptoms improve, targeting an initial 4 to 6 mmol/L rise. Overcorrection is treated with 5 percent dextrose infusion and desmopressin if the rate exceeds the ceiling.
key_points: Maximum sodium rise in 24 hours: 8 mmol/L (6 in elderly, hypokalaemic, chronic, malnourished)
Severe symptoms: 100 mL 3 percent saline bolus, may repeat every 10 min for symptomatic control
Overcorrection re-lowered with 5 percent dextrose and desmopressin
explanation.pearls: Osmotic demyelination classically manifests 2 to 6 days after overcorrection with pseudobulbar palsy, quadriparesis and locked-in state. Once occurred it is largely irreversible.

sources.label: Spasovski et al. European Society of Endocrinology Hyponatraemia Guideline. Eur J Endocrinol 2014

options.rationale: AU/international consensus recommends a maximum sodium rise of 8 mmol/L in 24 hours (some experts prefer 6 in high-risk groups: elderly, hypokalaemia, chronic hyponatraemia, malnutrition). Given severe symptoms, initial 100 mL 3 percent saline bolus is given, then repeat until symptoms improve, targeting an initial 4 to 6 mmol/L rise in the first few hours, but the 24-hour ceiling remains 8. (Source: European Society of Endocrinology Hyponatraemia Guideline; ANZ Renal Society)
Rapid correction exceeding 10 to 12 mmol/L per 24 hours substantially raises the risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome. This is unsafe. (Source: ANZ Renal Society Hyponatraemia Consensus)

Attempting to normalise sodium quickly is a classical error and directly causes osmotic demyelination. Immediate life-threatening features are addressed with a small bolus, not full normalisation. (Source: ANZ Renal Society Hyponatraemia Consensus)
She is not asymptomatic (drowsy, GCS 12) and 4 mmol/L is too conservative for a symptomatic presentation. The correct ceiling is 8 mmol/L. (Source: ANZ Renal Society Hyponatraemia Consensus)

The safety threshold is 10 mmol/L per 24 hours; most guidelines set a lower operating ceiling of 8 mmol/L to leave margin for error. 12 exceeds the safe range. (Source: ANZ Renal Society Hyponatraemia Consensus)

explanation.summary: Type A aortic dissection needs impulse control before pressure control: rate-limiting beta blocker first to blunt wall shear stress, then vasodilator to bring systolic blood pressure under 120 mmHg (measured in the higher arm). Emergency cardiothoracic surgery is definitive. Thrombolysis is contraindicated despite stroke features, which reflect innominate branch involvement rather than thromboembolic stroke.
key_points: Beta blocker FIRST for impulse control (target heart rate under 60), THEN vasodilator (target systolic under 120)
Thrombolysis and anticoagulation are contraindicated
Pericardiocentesis contraindicated in dissection with pericardial effusion without tamponade; if tamponade, only minimal drainage to restore perfusion until surgical repair
explanation.pearls: Measure blood pressure in the higher-reading arm to avoid under-treating on a compromised limb. A pulse deficit alone does not mean systemic hypotension.

sources.label: ANZ Society for Vascular Surgery Aortic Dissection Statement

options.rationale: Thrombolysis is contraindicated in aortic dissection because of the catastrophic haemorrhagic risk. The hemiparesis reflects innominate artery involvement, not thromboembolic stroke. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Aortic dissection)

Type A dissection medical management is impulse control: a rate-limiting beta blocker (esmolol or labetalol) FIRST to blunt shear stress, followed by a vasodilator to reduce blood pressure to a systolic under 120 mmHg (measured in the higher-reading arm). Reversing this order can cause reflex tachycardia and worsen dissection. (Source: ANZ Society for Vascular Surgery Aortic Dissection Statement; Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular)

Vasodilator without a rate-limiting agent causes reflex tachycardia and increased aortic wall shear stress, worsening dissection propagation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Aortic dissection)
Anticoagulation is contraindicated in acute aortic dissection because of haemorrhage risk into the false lumen and pericardium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Aortic dissection)

Pericardiocentesis in Type A dissection without tamponade is contraindicated because it can precipitate haemodynamic collapse from re-bleeding into the pericardium. Definitive treatment is emergency cardiothoracic surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Aortic dissection)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is diagnosed clinically and radiologically; the LRINEC score has poor negative predictive value and cannot rule it out when pretest probability is high (pain out of proportion, dusky skin, crepitus, and radiological gas are highly specific). Immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics with clindamycin (for toxin suppression) plus urgent surgical debridement are life-saving. Delay to imaging or scoring re-check increases mortality substantially.
key_points: High pretest probability features: pain out of proportion, dusky skin, crepitus, systemic toxicity, radiological subcutaneous gas
LRINEC is a decision-aid not a rule-out; borderline or low scores do not exclude the diagnosis
Empirical AU antibiotics: meropenem OR piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin for toxin suppression (add vancomycin if MRSA risk)
explanation.pearls: The clinical triage rule: if you are consulting surgery about NSTI, you are probably right. Delay to imaging is the commonest fatal error.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection
Stevens et al. IDSA Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

options.rationale: MRI is helpful when the diagnosis is uncertain but must NOT delay surgery when clinical and plain radiographic features are already diagnostic. Delay is directly associated with mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection

options.rationale: Flucloxacillin monotherapy is inadequate for polymicrobial necrotising soft tissue infection and does not provide toxin suppression. Marking and observation misses the operative window. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection

options.rationale: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a clinical and radiological diagnosis. The combination of pain out of proportion, dusky violaceous skin, subcutaneous crepitus, and radiological subcutaneous gas is highly specific despite a borderline LRINEC score. LRINEC has poor negative predictive value and should never delay surgery. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics with clindamycin (for toxin suppression) are given IMMEDIATELY but do not substitute for surgical debridement, which is the only definitive treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection

options.rationale: LRINEC is a decision-aid not a rule-out tool. A borderline or low score does not exclude necrotising fasciitis with high pretest probability. Delaying surgery is unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection

options.rationale: IVIG has an adjunctive role in streptococcal toxic shock syndrome once diagnosis is confirmed but does not replace surgery and antibiotics as first-line management of necrotising soft tissue infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection

explanation.summary: The modified Duke criteria define definite endocarditis with either (a) pathological criteria (culture or histology from vegetation or intracardiac abscess); (b) two major clinical criteria; (c) one major plus three minor; or (d) five minor. Major criteria are: typical organism in two or more separate blood cultures (or persistently positive) and evidence of endocardial involvement on echocardiography. Minor criteria include predisposition, fever, vascular phenomena, immunological phenomena, and microbiological evidence not meeting major. For IVDU tricuspid endocarditis, MSSA is most common; treatment is IV flucloxacillin 2 g four hourly for 2 to 6 weeks; TOE preferred over TTE for prosthetic valves and unclear TTE.
key_points: Duke: 2 majors, or 1 major + 3 minors, or 5 minors = definite.
IVDU tricuspid endocarditis most commonly MSSA.
Flucloxacillin 2 g IV 4 hourly for MSSA endocarditis.
TOE preferred to TTE for prosthetic valves or negative TTE with high suspicion.
explanation.pearls: Duke definite endocarditis by 2 major criteria: any typical organism in 2 or more separate cultures plus vegetation on echo; do not need pathology for the definite label.

sources.label: BSAC Duke criteria and endocarditis guidelines

options.rationale: Rejected requires firm alternative diagnosis or resolution with 4 days of antibiotics; this case is not rejected. (Source: BSAC Duke criteria; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Two major criteria (typical organism in two or more separate cultures plus positive echo with vegetation) equals definite endocarditis; empiric flucloxacillin (or benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin pending sensitivities) is standard. (Source: BSAC Duke criteria; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
This case fulfils two major criteria, not one; upgraded to definite classification. (Source: BSAC Duke criteria)
This route is a valid one for definite but not the classification here; two majors already suffice. (Source: BSAC Duke criteria)
The pulmonary nodules represent septic emboli from tricuspid endocarditis, not primary thromboembolic disease. (Source: BSAC Duke criteria)

explanation.summary: Empiric adult bacterial meningitis therapy in Australia is dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose, ceftriaxone 2 g IV twice daily (or cefotaxime 2 g IV six hourly) for pneumococcal and meningococcal cover, plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV four hourly for Listeria cover in patients over 50, immunocompromised, or with alcohol use. If suspected penicillin-resistant pneumococcus, add vancomycin 25 to 30 mg/kg. Dexamethasone reduces neurological sequelae and mortality in pneumococcal meningitis. LP should not delay antibiotics; CT before LP only if focal deficit, GCS reduction, seizure, or immunocompromise.
key_points: Empiric therapy above age 50: ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin plus dexamethasone.
Vancomycin added if penicillin-resistant pneumococcus suspected.
Dexamethasone before or with first antibiotic dose.
Do not delay antibiotics for imaging or LP.
explanation.pearls: Empiric adult meningitis above age 50: dexamethasone 10 mg IV, ceftriaxone 2 g IV BD, plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV four hourly for Listeria cover.

options.rationale: Missing benzylpenicillin misses Listeria cover which is essential above age 50 or in immunocompromised patients. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
This regimen misses ceftriaxone or cefotaxime which are cornerstone empiric cover for pneumococcal meningitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Metronidazole is not required for community meningitis and misses Listeria; benzylpenicillin plus a third generation cephalosporin is standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

eTG empiric bacterial meningitis above age 50: dexamethasone 10 mg with or before first antibiotic dose, then ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin (Listeria cover). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Antibiotics should not be delayed beyond 30 minutes for imaging or LP when meningitis is suspected; give empirically then image. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Osteoporosis in a man under 60 is secondary until proven otherwise. A secondary screen before treatment covers testosterone with sex hormone binding globulin and gonadotrophins, coeliac serology, serum and urine protein electrophoresis with free light chains, thyroid function, parathyroid hormone, corrected calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, renal and liver function and 25-hydroxy vitamin D. Alcohol intake, smoking and any past glucocorticoid or androgen deprivation therapy belong in the same assessment. Bisphosphonate treatment still goes ahead, but hypogonadism, coeliac disease and myeloma each need their own management. In context, the same screen applies to a premenopausal woman and to anyone whose bone density is much worse than their age and risk factors predict.
key_points: About half of men with osteoporosis have an identifiable secondary cause.
Screen for hypogonadism, coeliac disease and myeloma before treating.
Add thyroid function, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, liver and renal function.
A minimal trauma vertebral fracture confirms osteoporosis whatever the T-score.
explanation.pearls: An incidental wedge fracture on a chest or abdominal radiograph is a minimal trauma fracture and by itself justifies both treatment and the secondary screen.

sources.label: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia osteoporosis guideline

options.rationale: Around half of men with osteoporosis have a secondary cause, and hypogonadism, coeliac disease and myeloma are the ones that change management if found before an antiresorptive is started. (Source: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia osteoporosis guideline)
source_refs: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia osteoporosis guideline

options.rationale: Proceeding straight to an antiresorptive is reasonable in an older postmenopausal woman with a typical picture and normal screening bloods, but in a man this young it leaves a treatable cause running underneath. (Source: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia osteoporosis guideline)
source_refs: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia osteoporosis guideline

options.rationale: A bone scan is used to map Paget disease or to hunt for metastases, suggested by an isolated raised alkaline phosphatase or by bone pain with a known primary. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Interval densitometry is for monitoring an osteopenic result with no fracture; here the fracture and the T-score already establish the diagnosis and the need to treat. (Source: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia osteoporosis guideline)
source_refs: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia osteoporosis guideline

options.rationale: Bone biopsy is a specialist investigation reserved for suspected osteomalacia or renal bone disease that the biochemistry cannot resolve. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 hour-1 bundle: measure lactate, obtain blood cultures before antibiotics, administer broad spectrum antibiotics, start 30 mL/kg crystalloid within 3 hours for hypotension or lactate above 4 mmol/L, and apply vasopressors if MAP under 65 mmHg during or after fluid resuscitation. Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor; can start via a large peripheral vein while central access is being placed. Vasopressin is added second, then hydrocortisone for refractory shock. Bicarbonate is not used for pH above 7.15. Reassess lactate clearance to guide response.
key_points: 30 mL/kg crystalloid within 3 hours for hypotension or lactate above 4.
MAP target 65 mmHg; noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor.
Peripheral noradrenaline via large vein permitted while central sited.
Hydrocortisone for refractory vasopressor-requiring shock.
explanation.pearls: After 30 mL/kg crystalloid with persistent MAP under 65 mmHg, start noradrenaline peripherally via a large vein without waiting for central access.

options.rationale: After 30 mL/kg without target MAP achievement, further volume risks fluid overload; noradrenaline is Surviving Sepsis first-line vasopressor. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign; ANZICS)
Vasodilators worsen septic shock; the priority is vasoconstriction to restore MAP above 65 mmHg. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

MAP under 65 mmHg despite 30 mL/kg fluid meets Surviving Sepsis criteria for vasopressor; noradrenaline is first-line and can start peripherally via large vein. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; ANZICS)
Hydrocortisone is added when vasopressor requirement is significant despite adequate resuscitation, not before starting vasopressor. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Piperacillin-tazobactam is appropriate empiric cover for urosepsis; the immediate problem is haemodynamic failure requiring vasopressor. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency with hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and shock in an adrenally insufficient patient. Immediate treatment is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM followed by 200 mg per 24 hours (either as 50 mg every 6 hours IV or as an infusion) plus rapid isotonic fluid resuscitation. Precipitating illness (often infection or GI illness that prevents oral intake) needs concurrent treatment. Patients on chronic glucocorticoid replacement need sick-day rules: doubling oral hydrocortisone during minor illness, using parenteral hydrocortisone if unable to take oral, and going to hospital for vomiting despite injection. Prescribe injectable hydrocortisone emergency kit to all patients.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM immediately.
Follow with 200 mg per 24 hours plus isotonic fluid.
Do not delay for cortisol or Synacthen results.
Sick-day rules: double oral, parenteral if vomiting.
explanation.pearls: Suspected adrenal crisis: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM plus 0.9 percent sodium chloride immediately; investigate afterwards, not before treatment.

options.rationale: Adrenal crisis mandates immediate parenteral hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM plus rapid isotonic fluid resuscitation; do not delay for confirmatory tests. (Source: Endocrine Society; RACGP; AMH)
Diagnostic testing must not delay treatment of established adrenal crisis; give hydrocortisone first, then investigate. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)
Dexamethasone provides only glucocorticoid effect and no mineralocorticoid activity; hydrocortisone is preferred in known Addison's crisis. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)
Insulin and dextrose worsen hypoglycaemia and delay glucocorticoid; hyperkalaemia resolves with hydrocortisone and fluid resuscitation. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)
Oral therapy is unreliable in a vomiting hypotensive patient; adrenal crisis requires parenteral hydrocortisone immediately. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis features pain out of proportion to visible signs, rapid progression, systemic sepsis, dusky skin, bullae, and crepitus. LRINEC score uses CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose; a score of 6 or above raises suspicion, 8 or above strongly predicts. Definitive management is emergency surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics (typically meropenem plus clindamycin plus vancomycin) and ICU support. Delayed surgery is the strongest predictor of mortality. Imaging must not delay theatre when clinical suspicion is high. Group A streptococcus, Clostridium and polymicrobial infection are common causes.
key_points: Pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, dusky skin.
LRINEC 8 or above strongly predicts.
Emergency debridement within 6 hours plus broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Do not delay surgery for imaging.
explanation.pearls: Necrotising fasciitis with LRINEC 8 or above: theatre for wide debridement within 6 hours, meropenem plus clindamycin plus vancomycin, do not wait for imaging.

sources.label: ANZ Society for Vascular Surgery: Necrotising soft tissue infection

options.rationale: Cellulitis therapy alone with border marking delays surgical debridement, which is the definitive treatment; mortality rises sharply with delay. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; ANZ Society of Vascular Surgery)

LRINEC 8 or above with clinical features (pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, dusky skin) is necrotising fasciitis; urgent surgery within 6 hours is life-saving. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
HBO is an adjunct only; surgical debridement plus antibiotics is primary treatment and should not be delayed for HBO. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Bedside I and D is inadequate for necrotising fasciitis; theatre debridement to viable tissue with wide excision is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Imaging delays lifesaving surgery when clinical suspicion is high; go directly to theatre based on clinical and LRINEC findings. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: HHS is characterised by marked hyperglycaemia (usually above 30 mmol/L), hyperosmolality (above 320 mOsm/kg), and volume depletion without significant ketosis or acidosis. Fluid resuscitation is the mainstay: 1 litre 0.9 percent NaCl over 1 hour then 0.5 to 1 litre per hour for several hours, targeting glucose fall of 5 mmol/L per hour and sodium fall not exceeding 10 mmol/L in 24 hours. Insulin is delayed until glucose stops falling with fluid alone or ketones rise; a low dose (0.05 units/kg/hour) is used. Potassium replacement follows the same criteria as DKA. Complications include cerebral oedema (from rapid osmolar shifts), central pontine myelinolysis (from rapid sodium correction), and thromboembolism (heparin prophylaxis is standard). Mortality is 10 to 20 percent, higher than DKA.
key_points: HHS: glucose above 30, osmolality above 320, minimal ketosis.
First hour: 1 L 0.9 percent NaCl; do not start insulin yet.
Target glucose fall 5 mmol/L per hour by fluid alone.
Insulin 0.05 units/kg/hour only when glucose stops falling.
explanation.pearls: HHS first hour: 1 L 0.9 percent NaCl alone, no insulin until glucose fall stalls; unlike DKA, insulin is not part of the initial resuscitation because fluid alone typically drops glucose adequately.

options.rationale: In HHS insulin is delayed until fluid alone has brought glucose down 5 mmol/L per hour; immediate insulin risks cerebral oedema and cardiovascular collapse. (Source: JBDS-IP HHS; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
Hartmann's carries potassium load; JBDS uses 0.9 percent sodium chloride first-line for HHS with slow controlled rehydration. (Source: JBDS Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State)
Hypotonic fluid drops osmolality too fast in the first hour; 0.9 percent NaCl first, switch to 0.45 percent later if osmolality falls too slowly. (Source: JBDS Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State)
Adding dextrose before glucose falls below 14 mmol/L slows correction; do not add glucose in the first hours of HHS. (Source: JBDS Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State)

JBDS HHS pathway starts with 1 litre 0.9 percent NaCl over 1 hour, targeting glucose fall of 5 mmol/L per hour by fluid alone; insulin only if glucose is not falling. (Source: JBDS Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State)

explanation.summary: MTP is activated when massive haemorrhage is anticipated (typically more than 4 units of RBC in 1 hour, or expected total more than 10 units in 24 hours, or as clinically triggered by ongoing bleeding with coagulopathy). Products are delivered in balanced ratio (RBC to FFP to platelets 1:1:1) to prevent dilutional coagulopathy. Adjuncts: tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of injury (CRASH-2), cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate to keep fibrinogen above 1.5 to 2.0 g/L, calcium replacement to keep ionised calcium above 1.1 mmol/L (citrate binds calcium), warming to prevent the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy. Damage control resuscitation targets permissive hypotension (systolic 80 to 90 mmHg) until surgical control.
key_points: MTP: RBC:FFP:platelets 1:1:1 ratio plus TXA plus cryoprecipitate.
Tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 hours of injury (CRASH-2).
Keep fibrinogen above 1.5, ionised calcium above 1.1.
Permissive hypotension until surgical control.
explanation.pearls: Trauma MTP activation criteria: ongoing bleeding, 4 units RBC in 1 hour, INR above 1.5 or fibrinogen below 2, hypothermia below 35 degrees; deliver 1:1:1 ratio plus TXA plus cryoprecipitate from the outset.

options.rationale: Waiting until INR corrects worsens dilutional coagulopathy; MTP delivers RBC, FFP and platelets in balanced ratio from activation. (Source: NBA: Massive Transfusion; ANZICS)
TXA is essential but is not sufficient; ongoing haemorrhage with hypothermia, coagulopathy and acidosis warrants full MTP activation. (Source: NBA: Massive Transfusion)
Crystalloid worsens dilutional coagulopathy; blood product ratio therapy is preferred with permissive hypotension. (Source: NBA: Massive Transfusion)
Ongoing bleeding after 4 units RBC with coagulopathy, hypothermia, acidosis triggers MTP; 1:1:1 ratio plus TXA plus cryoprecipitate when fibrinogen below 2. (Source: NBA: Massive Transfusion)
PCC is reserved for warfarin or DOAC reversal, not trauma coagulopathy; balanced blood product ratio is the primary strategy. (Source: NBA: Massive Transfusion)

explanation.summary: Right-sided infective endocarditis in an IV drug user is characteristically caused by Staphylococcus aureus and typically involves the tricuspid valve with septic pulmonary emboli on chest imaging. Australian empirical therapy targets both MSSA and MRSA pending culture results: flucloxacillin plus vancomycin (loading dose then weight-based maintenance). Once organism and sensitivities are known, therapy is narrowed: flucloxacillin monotherapy for MSSA, vancomycin monotherapy for MRSA. Duration is at least 4 weeks IV for uncomplicated right-sided IE, longer for complications. Echocardiography (transthoracic first, transoesophageal if inconclusive or valve surgery being considered) is essential.
key_points: Right-sided IE in IVDU is usually Staph aureus.
Empirical cover: flucloxacillin plus vancomycin for MSSA and MRSA.
Narrow to flucloxacillin (MSSA) or vancomycin (MRSA) on sensitivities.
Uncomplicated right-sided IE requires 4 weeks IV therapy.
explanation.pearls: In an IV drug user with fevers, pulmonary infiltrates and a tricuspid murmur, start empirical flucloxacillin plus vancomycin after two sets of blood cultures; do not use ceftriaxone monotherapy or oral therapy.

options.rationale: Right-sided IE in an IV drug user is usually Staphylococcus aureus; empirical therapy targets MSSA and MRSA together (flucloxacillin plus vancomycin) until sensitivities are known. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

This is the empirical regimen for native-valve left-sided community-onset endocarditis without staphylococcal risk factors; it undertreats staphylococcal disease in an IV drug user. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)
Oral therapy is inappropriate for endocarditis; parenteral therapy is required until bactericidal control is documented. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

Piperacillin-tazobactam does not adequately cover MRSA and is not the standard empirical regimen for IE; staphylococcal cover is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)
Ceftriaxone monotherapy does not cover staphylococci adequately and misses MRSA in an IV drug user population. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

explanation.summary: The Australian HIV testing algorithm during suspected acute seroconversion uses HIV RNA (viral load) PCR to detect infection during the antibody window period. Fourth-generation antibody-antigen combined assays detect p24 antigen from around 14 to 21 days post-exposure and antibody from 20 to 45 days. HIV RNA becomes detectable earliest, from around 10 days post-exposure. Symptomatic acute seroconversion presents with a mononucleosis-like illness (fever, pharyngitis, rash, lymphadenopathy, myalgia) and represents the period of highest transmission risk. Positive RNA testing should be followed by confirmatory testing and immediate linkage to specialist care and antiretroviral therapy initiation.
key_points: HIV RNA is detectable from around 10 days post-exposure.
Fourth-generation antibody-antigen from 2 to 3 weeks; antibody from 3 to 6 weeks.
Symptomatic seroconversion is the period of highest transmission risk.
Positive RNA triggers immediate linkage to specialist care.
explanation.pearls: In a mononucleosis-like illness with recent condomless anal sex and negative combined assay, order HIV RNA PCR immediately rather than waiting for antibody seroconversion.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV Medicine (ASHM) Guidelines

options.rationale: The clinical picture is highly suggestive of acute HIV seroconversion; waiting 8 weeks delays diagnosis while transmission risk is highest. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)
Western blot detects antibody, which lags viral RNA; a negative combined assay implies Western blot would also be negative in the window period. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)
CD4 counts are not diagnostic in acute infection; they are used for staging established disease and monitoring therapy. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)
EBV remains a differential but does not rule out acute HIV; failing to test for HIV RNA in this clinical picture would miss primary infection. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)

HIV RNA becomes detectable around 10 days post-exposure, before p24 antigen and antibody; RNA is the diagnostic test during the antibody window in symptomatic seroconversion. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a surgical emergency and diagnosis is primarily clinical. Features raising suspicion include severe pain out of proportion, dusky skin changes, bullae, crepitus, cutaneous anaesthesia, systemic toxicity and rapid progression. The LRINEC score uses CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose to stratify risk; score 6 or above is high probability of NSTI. Definitive treatment is early aggressive surgical debridement combined with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem, plus vancomycin, plus clindamycin for toxin suppression). Imaging must not delay surgery.
key_points: Diagnosis of NSTI is clinical; LRINEC assists risk stratification.
LRINEC 6 or above is high probability.
Surgical debridement is definitive treatment.
Empirical antibiotics: piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin plus clindamycin.
explanation.pearls: In a diabetic with pain out of proportion, dusky calf skin, bullae and LRINEC 6 or above, call the surgeon before you order the CT scan; delayed debridement is the leading cause of mortality.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue

options.rationale: The presentation is high probability necrotising soft tissue infection (LRINEC 8); oral outpatient therapy is inappropriate and fatal delay is likely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue

options.rationale: LRINEC score 6 or above is high probability necrotising fasciitis; urgent surgical debridement is the definitive treatment along with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue

options.rationale: Imaging must not delay surgery when clinical suspicion is high; MRI has a role only if surgical decision is genuinely uncertain and delay is not harmful. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue

options.rationale: Vancomycin monotherapy misses gram-negative and anaerobic cover; NSTI requires triple-agent empirical therapy plus surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue

options.rationale: Biopsy has no acute diagnostic role; deep tissue samples are taken intraoperatively. Delay to biopsy would be fatal in NSTI. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a life-threatening emergency in known Addison's disease, often triggered by intercurrent illness or failure of sick-day dose adjustment. Immediate treatment is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg over 24 hours (either continuous infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours), together with 1 litre of 0.9 percent sodium chloride over the first hour and glucose replacement for hypoglycaemia. Hydrocortisone provides both glucocorticoid and adequate mineralocorticoid activity at these doses so separate fludrocortisone is not needed until doses drop below 50 mg per day. Patients should be educated on sick-day rules (double oral dose for febrile illness, IM hydrocortisone if vomiting).
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours.
Hydrocortisone provides mineralocorticoid activity at these doses.
IV fluids: 1 litre 0.9 percent sodium chloride in the first hour.
Sick-day rules: double oral dose or IM hydrocortisone if vomiting.
explanation.pearls: In known Addison's disease with vomiting and hypotension, give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately and 1 litre normal saline in the first hour before any workup; dexamethasone is reserved for undiagnosed cases going for synacthen testing.

options.rationale: Oral steroids are inappropriate when the patient is vomiting; parenteral hydrocortisone is required and prednisolone lacks the mineralocorticoid activity of hydrocortisone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal crisis)

Fludrocortisone is not the acute treatment; glucocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone) is urgent and the patient is vomiting so oral therapy is inappropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal crisis)

Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and hydrocortisone is preferred; dexamethasone is used only if the diagnosis is uncertain and short synacthen test is planned. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal crisis)

Vasopressors are refractory to steroid deficiency; hydrocortisone must be given first and vasopressors are used only if BP remains inadequate after fluids and steroids. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal crisis)

Adrenal crisis management is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours (or 50 mg every 6 hours) alongside IV fluid resuscitation and glucose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal crisis)

explanation.summary: Guillain-Barre syndrome is treated with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, both of which shorten recovery when given within 4 weeks of symptom onset. Neither corticosteroids alone nor a combination of IVIG and PLEX improve outcomes. Australian standard therapy is IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days. Respiratory monitoring is critical: forced vital capacity under 20 mL/kg, negative inspiratory force weaker than -30 cmH2O or vital capacity fall over 30 percent from baseline signal impending respiratory failure and are indications for early ICU transfer and elective intubation. Autonomic instability and dysautonomia must be watched for.
key_points: IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days is equivalent to PLEX.
Steroids are not effective in acute GBS.
FVC under 20 mL/kg triggers ICU and intubation consideration.
Autonomic dysfunction is common; continuous cardiac monitoring required.
explanation.pearls: In GBS with FVC under 25 mL/kg, start IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days and transfer to a monitored bed; steroids do not help and combined IVIG plus PLEX offers no advantage.

options.rationale: Corticosteroids are not effective in Guillain-Barre syndrome and may worsen outcomes; IVIG or plasma exchange are the treatments of choice. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)

IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days is equivalent to plasma exchange in accelerating recovery when started within 4 weeks of onset; IVIG is generally preferred for ease of administration and availability. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)
Combining IVIG and PLEX does not improve outcomes over either alone and increases cost and complications; single-modality therapy is standard. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)

Long-term immunosuppression is used for chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP), not acute GBS; acute treatment is short-course IVIG or PLEX. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)

Supportive care alone underserves patients with rapidly progressive disease or respiratory compromise; immunotherapy shortens recovery time and reduces disability. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)

explanation.summary: Methotrexate is first-line disease-modifying therapy for rheumatoid arthritis in Australia when there is no contraindication. Starting dose is 10 to 15 mg orally once weekly, escalated to 20 to 25 mg weekly as tolerated over 8 to 12 weeks, with folic acid 5 mg weekly on a different day to reduce side effects. Pre-treatment screening covers hepatitis B and C serology, latent TB (QuantiFERON), liver function, renal function and chest X-ray. Bridging low-dose prednisolone may be used for symptomatic control during DMARD onset. Biologics are added when conventional DMARDs fail; PBS eligibility requires demonstrated failure of methotrexate and one other conventional DMARD.
key_points: Methotrexate is first-line RA DMARD in Australia.
Starting dose 10 to 15 mg weekly with folic acid 5 mg different day.
Pre-screen: hepatitis B/C, QuantiFERON, LFT, U/E, CXR.
Biologics after conventional DMARD failure per PBS criteria.
explanation.pearls: For new RA with high disease activity and no contraindication, start methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid 5 mg on a different day; biologics come only after conventional DMARD failure under PBS rules.

options.rationale: Sulfasalazine is a DMARD alternative for methotrexate-intolerant or pregnancy-planning patients; it is not the standard first-line agent when methotrexate is safe. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association Consensus)
Hydroxychloroquine monotherapy is inadequate for moderate to high disease activity; methotrexate is preferred as first-line. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association Consensus)

Biologics are used after inadequate response to conventional DMARDs; PBS eligibility requires demonstrated failure of methotrexate plus at least one other conventional DMARD. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association Consensus)

Australian consensus (ARA) makes methotrexate first-line for RA when there is no contraindication; starting dose 10 to 15 mg weekly with folic acid 5 mg on a different day reduces gastrointestinal and mucosal side effects. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association Consensus)

Chronic corticosteroid monotherapy is not disease-modifying long-term and carries significant harms; steroids may be used as short-term bridge alongside DMARD initiation. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association Consensus)

explanation.summary: Warfarin-associated major bleeding, including intracranial haemorrhage, is reversed with intravenous vitamin K plus a prothrombin complex concentrate. In Australia, prothrombinex-VF (three-factor PCC containing factors II, IX and X) is the standard product, dosed at 25 to 50 IU/kg IV depending on the INR and clinical urgency, with concurrent IV vitamin K 5 to 10 mg for durable reversal. Fresh frozen plasma may be added if factor VII replacement is needed. Repeat INR is measured 30 to 60 minutes after prothrombinex-VF to confirm reversal. Definitive management includes blood pressure control (target systolic under 140 mmHg for spontaneous ICH per INTERACT2) and neurosurgical review.
key_points: Prothrombinex-VF 25 to 50 IU/kg plus vitamin K 5 to 10 mg IV.
FFP is second-line or adjunct for factor VII replacement.
Vitamin K essential for durable reversal (short PCC half-life).
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran; andexanet alfa reverses xabans.
explanation.pearls: In warfarin-associated ICH, give prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg plus IV vitamin K 10 mg immediately and control blood pressure to systolic under 140 mmHg; FFP alone or oral vitamin K is too slow.

options.rationale: Oral vitamin K is too slow (12 to 24 hours) and FFP is slower and less effective than prothrombinex-VF for warfarin-associated intracranial haemorrhage; IV vitamin K and prothrombinex-VF are indicated. (Source: Australian Blood Authority: Warfarin reversal)

FFP is second-line reversal because volume load and time-to-normalise INR are inferior to prothrombinex-VF; vitamin K is also essential for durable reversal. (Source: Australian Blood Authority: Warfarin reversal)
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, not warfarin; it has no role here. (Source: Australian Blood Authority: Warfarin reversal)

Recombinant factor VIIa is not standard warfarin reversal and carries thromboembolic risk; prothrombinex-VF is the preferred product for warfarin-related intracranial bleeding. (Source: Australian Blood Authority: Warfarin reversal)

For life-threatening warfarin-associated bleeding, Australian standard is prothrombinex-VF (three-factor PCC) 25 to 50 IU/kg IV plus vitamin K 5 to 10 mg IV; FFP is added if factor VII replacement is needed for full correction. (Source: Australian Blood Authority: Warfarin reversal)

explanation.summary: Unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis carries a substantial long-term recurrence risk (around 10 percent in the first year off treatment, 30 percent at 5 years) and Australian guidance supports indefinite anticoagulation unless the patient has high bleeding risk. Reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily after the initial 6 months of full-dose treatment is supported by the AMPLIFY-EXT trial and reduces recurrence with bleeding rates comparable to placebo. Full-dose continuation (apixaban 5 mg BD or rivaroxaban 20 mg daily) is also acceptable. Aspirin is inferior to apixaban but is an option when anticoagulation is refused or contraindicated. Reassessment of bleeding risk should be periodic.
key_points: Unprovoked proximal DVT recurrence: 10 percent in year 1 off Rx.
Indefinite anticoagulation recommended when bleeding risk is low.
Reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg BD after 6 months per AMPLIFY-EXT.
Aspirin is inferior to apixaban for extended prevention.
explanation.pearls: After 6 months for unprovoked proximal DVT, continue indefinite anticoagulation and consider stepping down to apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily; do not stop at 6 months and do not switch to aspirin.

options.rationale: Unprovoked proximal DVT carries a recurrence risk of around 10 percent in the first year and 30 percent at 5 years after stopping; indefinite anticoagulation is recommended unless bleeding risk is high. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - VTE)

The AMPLIFY-EXT trial supports reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg BD after 6 months, but this is one option; full-dose continuation is also acceptable. However indefinite continuation is what is indicated - the specific dose regimen is a secondary decision. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - VTE)

For unprovoked proximal DVT with low bleeding risk, indefinite anticoagulation is recommended; reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg BD after the initial treatment period is supported by AMPLIFY-EXT and reduces recurrence with comparable bleeding to placebo. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - VTE)
Aspirin is inferior to reduced-dose apixaban for VTE recurrence prevention; it is an option only when anticoagulation is refused or contraindicated. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - VTE)

There is no advantage to switching from apixaban to warfarin unless there is a specific indication (mechanical valve, severe renal impairment); DOACs are preferred in Australian guidance for uncomplicated VTE. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - VTE)

explanation.summary: Severe ANCA-associated vasculitis with organ-threatening disease (renal, pulmonary, neurological) requires combination induction with a cytotoxic or biologic agent plus glucocorticoids. Rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 weeks) plus glucocorticoids has become the preferred regimen in most centres based on RAVE and RITUXVAS; it is at least equivalent to cyclophosphamide for induction and is preferred when fertility preservation matters, prior cyclophosphamide exposure exists, or in PR3-ANCA disease where relapse rates are higher and rituximab retreatment is more feasible. Plasma exchange is reserved for severe pulmonary haemorrhage or dialysis-dependent renal failure; PEXIVAS reduced routine indications. Maintenance is with rituximab or azathioprine.
key_points: Severe ANCA vasculitis requires combination induction, not steroid alone.
Rituximab plus steroid is at least equivalent to cyclophosphamide.
Rituximab preferred for fertility, prior cyclophosphamide, PR3 positivity.
Plasma exchange reserved for severe pulmonary haemorrhage or dialysis need.
explanation.pearls: In new severe PR3-positive ANCA vasculitis with pulmonary-renal syndrome, induce with rituximab plus glucocorticoids rather than cyclophosphamide when fertility, prior exposure or relapse risk favours it.

options.rationale: Steroid monotherapy is inadequate induction for severe ANCA vasculitis with organ-threatening disease; a cytotoxic agent or rituximab is required. (Source: KDIGO Glomerulonephritis Guideline 2021)

Rituximab plus glucocorticoids is at least equivalent to cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoids for induction in severe ANCA vasculitis and is preferred where fertility preservation, prior cyclophosphamide exposure or PR3 positivity applies; RITUXVAS and RAVE support this. (Source: KDIGO Glomerulonephritis Guideline 2021)

Plasma exchange is an adjunct in severe pulmonary haemorrhage or dialysis-dependent renal failure and is not standalone induction; PEXIVAS reduced enthusiasm for routine use. (Source: KDIGO Glomerulonephritis Guideline 2021)

Oral cyclophosphamide is a legitimate induction regimen but is less used since rituximab became available; IV pulsed cyclophosphamide or rituximab is preferred to minimise cumulative toxicity. (Source: KDIGO Glomerulonephritis Guideline 2021)
Methotrexate is used for non-organ-threatening disease; it is inadequate for severe ANCA vasculitis with renal or pulmonary involvement. (Source: KDIGO Glomerulonephritis Guideline 2021)

explanation.summary: Atypical femoral fracture is a rare complication of prolonged antiresorptive therapy that announces itself weeks to months in advance with dull groin or thigh pain. Plain radiographs of both femurs, including the full shaft, show lateral cortical thickening with a transverse beaking lucency; if they are normal and suspicion persists, magnetic resonance imaging or a bone scan is the next test. The bisphosphonate is stopped, calcium and vitamin D are continued, and an incomplete fracture is referred for orthopaedic assessment and usually prophylactic intramedullary nailing. In context, this is the main reason the benefit of bisphosphonate treatment is reviewed at around five years, with a drug holiday for those whose fracture risk has fallen and continuation for those still at high risk.
key_points: Prodromal thigh or groin pain precedes most atypical femoral fractures.
Image both femurs, including the full shaft, because lesions are often bilateral.
Stop the bisphosphonate and refer an incomplete fracture for orthopaedic review.
Absolute risk remains low and far smaller than the fractures prevented.
explanation.pearls: Atypical fractures are transverse, start in the lateral cortex and occur with minimal or no trauma, which is what separates them from a typical intertrochanteric or subcapital fracture after a fall.

sources.label: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia osteoporosis guideline

options.rationale: Prodromal thigh or groin pain after years of bisphosphonate treatment is an incomplete atypical femoral fracture until imaging says otherwise, and the contralateral femur is imaged because the lesions are often bilateral. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Physiotherapy suits mechanical hip or trochanteric pain that is movement related and settles with rest, not pain that has become constant on long term antiresorptive therapy. (Source: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia osteoporosis guideline)
source_refs: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia osteoporosis guideline

options.rationale: Spinal imaging is indicated when the pain follows a dermatome, radiates below the knee, or comes with neurological signs, none of which are described. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
Changing antiresorptive class is considered for intolerance or renal impairment, but denosumab carries the same atypical fracture risk and a switch leaves the femur unimaged. (Source: AMH)

Analgesia alone is appropriate for a self-limiting musculoskeletal strain with a clear mechanism; waiting here risks the incomplete fracture progressing to a complete one. (Source: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia osteoporosis guideline)
source_refs: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia osteoporosis guideline

explanation.summary: For a first unprovoked proximal DVT or PE, at least 3 months of full-dose anticoagulation is mandatory. Beyond 3 months, decisions balance annual recurrence (about 10 percent per year unprovoked, cumulative 30 percent at 5 years) against bleeding risk. In low bleeding risk (HAS-BLED under 3, no active bleeding, no recent GI bleed), extended prevention with reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg BD or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily reduces recurrence with comparable bleeding to placebo (AMPLIFY-EXT, EINSTEIN-CHOICE). Provoked VTE by a major transient risk factor completes 3 months and stops. Cancer-associated VTE continues while cancer is active.
key_points: First unprovoked VTE: minimum 3 months full-dose therapy.
Extended prevention: apixaban 2.5 mg BD or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily.
Aspirin is inferior to DOAC for extended prevention.
Provoked VTE by major transient factor: 3 months and stop.
explanation.pearls: Unprovoked proximal DVT with low bleeding risk after 6 months full-dose apixaban: step down to 2.5 mg BD extended prevention (AMPLIFY-EXT); aspirin monotherapy is inferior.

options.rationale: Full-dose extended anticoagulation is one option but current AU guidance supports reduced-dose apixaban after 6 months in unprovoked VTE with low bleeding risk. (Source: THANZ position statement: VTE)
Switching to warfarin adds monitoring burden and offers no efficacy advantage over reduced-dose apixaban for extended prevention. (Source: THANZ position statement: VTE)
Aspirin is inferior to a reduced-dose DOAC for extended VTE prevention and does not match the recurrence reduction achieved with apixaban 2.5 mg BD. (Source: THANZ position statement: VTE)

After at least 6 months of full-dose therapy, extended reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily reduces recurrent VTE while limiting bleeding in low-risk patients - the AMPLIFY-EXT strategy. (Source: THANZ position statement: VTE)

Ceasing anticoagulation after 3 months in unprovoked VTE with low bleeding risk carries an annual recurrence risk near 10 percent; extended prevention is preferred. (Source: THANZ position statement: VTE)

explanation.summary: Australian first-line treatment for postmenopausal osteoporosis with a minimal trauma fracture is an oral bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly / 150 mg monthly) with adequate calcium (1300 mg/day) and vitamin D (25-OH above 50 nmol/L). Zoledronic acid 5 mg IV yearly is an alternative for intolerance of oral therapy. Denosumab is second-line and requires an exit strategy (bisphosphonate cover) to prevent multiple vertebral fractures on discontinuation. Teriparatide is PBS reserved for severe osteoporosis with multiple fractures despite antiresorptives. Assess dental health, renal function and vitamin D before initiation.
key_points: First-line: oral alendronate or risedronate + calcium + vitamin D.
Denosumab is second-line and needs an exit strategy.
Teriparatide: severe osteoporosis with failure of antiresorptive.
Strontium ranelate withdrawn in Australia.
explanation.pearls: Postmenopausal minimal trauma fracture with T-score -3.1 starts oral alendronate 70 mg weekly with calcium 1300 mg/day and 25-OH vitamin D above 50 nmol/L; check creatinine clearance stays above 35.

options.rationale: Strontium ranelate has been withdrawn from the Australian market due to cardiovascular safety concerns. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis guideline)

Denosumab is second-line in AU or first-line only when bisphosphonates are contraindicated or not tolerated; it also carries a rebound fracture risk on cessation. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis guideline)
Teriparatide is PBS reserved for severe osteoporosis with multiple minimal trauma fractures despite prior antiresorptive therapy. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis guideline)
MHT is not first-line for osteoporosis treatment; bone benefit ceases on stopping and there are alternative safer antiresorptive options. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis guideline)

Oral alendronate is the AU first-line agent for postmenopausal osteoporosis with minimal trauma fracture, meets PBS criteria and is well tolerated with normal creatinine clearance. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis guideline)

explanation.summary: Falls prevention in older adults requires multifactorial assessment: vision, hearing, gait/balance, footwear, home hazards, orthostatic blood pressure, comorbidity optimisation and medication review. STOPP-Frail identifies high-risk medications for deprescribing: benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, tricyclic antidepressants, first-generation antihistamines, anticholinergics (oxybutynin, tolterodine), opioids, typical antipsychotics, and unnecessary antihypertensives. Benzodiazepines and TCAs have the strongest evidence for falls reduction on cessation. Taper gradually to avoid withdrawal, and coordinate with non-pharmacological strategies (physiotherapy-led balance training, home OT assessment).
key_points: Multifactorial assessment underlies falls prevention.
Highest-risk medications: benzodiazepines, TCAs, anticholinergics.
Deprescribing must be gradual to avoid withdrawal.
Combine with balance training and home OT review.
explanation.pearls: In a falling older adult on both temazepam and amitriptyline, plan a coordinated taper and cessation of both as the first-line intervention; benzodiazepines and TCAs are the top STOPP-Frail falls targets.

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines and tricyclics are the highest-risk STOPP-Frail deprescribing targets in older adults with recurrent falls; both should be tapered and stopped as the priority. (Source: RACGP Aged care - Deprescribing)
The orthostatic drop is modest and not the highest-yield falls target; benzodiazepines and TCAs have larger evidence for falls reduction on cessation. (Source: RACGP Aged care - Deprescribing)
Statin-related myopathy is uncommon and does not typically cause falls; benzodiazepines and TCAs are far higher priority for falls in the elderly. (Source: RACGP Aged care - Deprescribing)
Metformin does not cause hypoglycaemia; his HbA1c is well-controlled and the risk is negligible for falls contribution. (Source: RACGP Aged care - Deprescribing)
Increasing an anticholinergic worsens central adverse effects and falls risk in the elderly; oxybutynin itself is a deprescribing target. (Source: RACGP Aged care - Deprescribing)

explanation.summary: Australian HIV guidance (ASHM) recommends antiretroviral therapy for all people living with HIV regardless of CD4 count, with rapid start (ideally within 7 days of diagnosis) once baseline safety labs and hepatitis screening are back. Preferred first-line regimens are single-tablet integrase inhibitor based combinations: bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (BIC/FTC/TAF) or dolutegravir with lamivudine (2-drug) or dolutegravir with tenofovir/emtricitabine (3-drug). Abacavir-based regimens require HLA-B*5701 negative status. Undetectable viral load equals untransmittable (U equals U) and is the treatment goal. Baseline resistance testing is performed but does not delay treatment initiation.
key_points: ART is recommended for all PLHIV regardless of CD4.
Rapid start ideally within 7 days of diagnosis.
First-line: integrase inhibitor STR (BIC/FTC/TAF).
Abacavir requires HLA-B*5701 negative.
explanation.pearls: New HIV diagnosis with hepatitis B and HLA-B*5701 negative: start BIC/FTC/TAF single tablet within days, do not wait for CD4 threshold or full resistance report before initiation.

options.rationale: Deferring ART is superseded; ART is recommended for all HIV-positive adults regardless of CD4 count in Australia. (Source: ASHM Australian Consensus HIV guidelines)

Rapid start of a preferred integrase-inhibitor based single-tablet regimen (bictegravir/emtricitabine/TAF) is standard in Australia once baseline results permit safe initiation. (Source: ASHM Australian Consensus HIV guidelines)

Efavirenz has neuropsychiatric side effects and is no longer first-line; integrase inhibitor based regimens (bictegravir, dolutegravir) are preferred. (Source: ASHM Australian Consensus HIV guidelines)
Monotherapy is inadequate; the AU standard remains a three-drug regimen or a validated two-drug regimen with NRTI backbone, not monotherapy. (Source: ASHM Australian Consensus HIV guidelines)
Abacavir requires HLA-B*5701 negative status before initiation to avoid hypersensitivity syndrome; typing must be done before starting. (Source: ASHM Australian Consensus HIV guidelines)

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection (positive IGRA or TST without symptoms, signs or radiographic evidence of active disease) is treated in adults at increased risk of reactivation (healthcare workers, HIV, TNF inhibitor users, close contacts). Preferred CDNA/NTAC regimens are: isoniazid + rifapentine weekly for 12 doses (3HP), isoniazid daily for 6 or 9 months (6H or 9H), rifampicin daily for 4 months (4R), or isoniazid + rifampicin for 3 or 4 months (3HR/4HR). 3HP has the best completion rates. Rifamycin interactions with combined oral contraception are important - counsel on additional contraception.
key_points: 3HP (isoniazid + rifapentine 12 weeks) is preferred for completion.
6H or 9H isoniazid daily are alternatives.
Rifampicin interacts with oral contraceptives.
Baseline and monitoring LFTs required.
explanation.pearls: Positive IGRA healthcare worker with clear chest X-ray and normal LFTs: 3HP (weekly isoniazid + rifapentine for 12 doses under directly observed therapy) is the preferred short-course regimen.

options.rationale: Rifampicin monotherapy for 4 months (4R) is an alternative but interacts strongly with combined oral contraceptives - counselling and additional contraception are required; 3HP is preferred here. (Source: CDNA/NTAC latent TB guidance)
12 months of dual therapy exceeds evidence-based durations for latent TB; short-course regimens are preferred. (Source: CDNA/NTAC latent TB guidance)

Short-course rifapentine plus isoniazid for 12 weeks (3HP) is a preferred CDNA/NTAC regimen for latent TB in adults with good adherence, matching daily 9-month isoniazid for efficacy at lower duration. (Source: CDNA/NTAC latent TB guidance)
Active TB treatment is not indicated in latent infection; asymptomatic with clear CXR excludes active disease. (Source: CDNA/NTAC latent TB guidance)
Untreated latent TB in a healthcare worker carries a 5 to 10 percent lifetime reactivation risk; treatment is indicated per CDNA/NTAC. (Source: CDNA/NTAC latent TB guidance)

explanation.summary: Early rheumatoid arthritis (symptom duration under 6 months, seropositive with anti-CCP, elevated inflammatory markers, symmetric small joint involvement) benefits from disease-modifying therapy within 3 months of onset - the window of opportunity. Methotrexate is the AU/international anchor drug: start 10-15 mg weekly PO with folic acid 5 mg weekly. Bridging low-dose prednisolone (10-15 mg tapered over 6-8 weeks) controls symptoms while methotrexate takes effect. Baseline FBC, LFTs, renal function, hepatitis B and C screening, and chest X-ray are required before start. Biologic DMARDs (TNF inhibitors, JAK inhibitors) are second-line after csDMARD failure.
key_points: Window of opportunity: DMARD within 3 months of onset.
Methotrexate 10-15 mg weekly + folic acid is anchor therapy.
Bridging prednisolone taper covers slow methotrexate onset.
Baseline hepatitis, TB and chest X-ray screening before start.
explanation.pearls: Early seropositive symmetric small joint synovitis with anti-CCP 108 and CRP 48 warrants methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid and urgent rheumatology referral; do not wait 6 weeks for the specialist appointment.

options.rationale: Six-week deferral risks irreversible joint damage; the window-of-opportunity concept supports DMARD start within 3 months. (Source: ARA rheumatoid arthritis guideline)
Steroid monotherapy without DMARD cover allows joint damage to progress; DMARD should not be delayed by weeks awaiting specialist review. (Source: ARA rheumatoid arthritis guideline)
NSAIDs treat symptoms but do not prevent erosive joint damage; disease-modifying therapy is required in early RA. (Source: ARA rheumatoid arthritis guideline)

Early RA benefits from DMARD initiation within 3 months of symptom onset; methotrexate is the anchor drug and can be started while awaiting specialist review per RACGP/ARA guidance. (Source: ARA rheumatoid arthritis guideline)
Biologic DMARDs are reserved for failure of conventional synthetic DMARDs and require rheumatologist-led initiation with screening. (Source: ARA rheumatoid arthritis guideline)

explanation.summary: Migraine prophylaxis is indicated for 4 or more monthly migraine days, or fewer episodes that significantly impair function. Australian eTG first-line agents are propranolol (first-line if no contraindication), amitriptyline (preferred if asthma, comorbid tension headache or insomnia), topiramate, sodium valproate (contraindicated in women of childbearing age without strict pregnancy prevention), pizotifen and candesartan. Newer CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab) are PBS-listed for refractory chronic migraine after failure of 3 prior classes. Trial each agent for 8-12 weeks at target dose before considering failure.
key_points: Prophylaxis threshold: 4+ migraine days per month or significant impairment.
Propranolol is first-line unless asthma, brady, hypotension.
Amitriptyline is preferred with asthma or insomnia comorbidity.
Valproate is contraindicated in women of childbearing age.
explanation.pearls: Frequent migraine in an asthmatic woman: skip propranolol, choose amitriptyline 10 mg nocte titrated to 25-50 mg; trial for 8-12 weeks before deeming ineffective.

sources.label: Australian Headache Society: Migraine management position statement

options.rationale: Propranolol is usually first-line migraine prophylaxis, but is relatively contraindicated in moderate persistent asthma and a non-cardioselective beta-blocker may worsen bronchospasm. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine)

Regular daily paracetamol risks medication overuse headache and is not effective prophylaxis; prophylactic therapy needs a targeted evidence-based agent. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine)

Valproate is effective for migraine prophylaxis but is contraindicated in women of childbearing age unless pregnancy prevention criteria are strictly met due to teratogenicity risk. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine)
Verapamil is used for cluster headache prophylaxis rather than migraine; it lacks the evidence base of TCAs, beta-blockers or topiramate for migraine. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine)

In a patient where beta-blocker is unsuitable (moderate persistent asthma), amitriptyline is a preferred first-line migraine prophylactic per Australian eTG. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine)

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome is investigated stepwise: confirm hypercortisolism biochemically before any imaging or localisation. First-line screening tests (any two positive out of three, or one strongly positive with high clinical suspicion) are 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression (cortisol under 50 nmol/L excludes), 24-hour urinary free cortisol (2-3 collections), and late-night salivary cortisol (loss of diurnal rhythm). Once confirmed, plasma ACTH distinguishes ACTH-dependent (pituitary or ectopic) from ACTH-independent (adrenal) aetiology, then imaging directs pituitary vs ectopic vs adrenal disease. Inferior petrosal sinus sampling is reserved for ACTH-dependent cases with equivocal pituitary MRI.
key_points: Confirm hypercortisolism before any imaging.
1 mg DST, 24-hour urine free cortisol, late-night salivary are screens.
ACTH after confirmation distinguishes dependent from independent.
IPSS for equivocal ACTH-dependent pituitary MRI.
explanation.pearls: Suspected Cushing: start with 1 mg overnight DST and 08:00 cortisol; only after confirmed hypercortisolism measure ACTH and image.

options.rationale: 1 mg overnight DST is a preferred Endocrine Society and Australian first-line screen for suspected Cushing syndrome; a morning cortisol above 50 nmol/L suggests failure of suppression and warrants further investigation. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline)
ACTH is used to distinguish ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent Cushing after diagnosis is established, not as a screening test. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline)
IPSS is a highly specialised test for distinguishing pituitary from ectopic ACTH after Cushing is confirmed and ACTH-dependent aetiology established. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline)
Random cortisol is unreliable due to diurnal variation; screening uses 1 mg DST, 24 hour urinary free cortisol or late-night salivary cortisol. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline)
Imaging before biochemistry generates incidentaloma noise (adrenal nodules are common); biochemical confirmation must come first. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline)

explanation.summary: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a progressive fibrotic interstitial lung disease diagnosed by an ILD multidisciplinary team using HRCT and clinical assessment. Definite UIP pattern on HRCT (basal and peripheral reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, no atypical features) in an appropriate clinical context does not require surgical lung biopsy.
