Antifibrotic therapy (pirfenidone or nintedanib) slows FVC decline and is PBS-listed for FVC 50-80 percent predicted and DLCO 30-79 percent predicted. Non-pharmacological care includes pulmonary rehabilitation, smoking cessation, oxygen for hypoxaemia, vaccinations, and early lung transplant referral for suitable candidates.
key_points: Definite HRCT UIP + clinical context = IPF diagnosis without biopsy.
Antifibrotics (pirfenidone or nintedanib) slow FVC decline.
PBS criteria: FVC 50-80 and DLCO 30-79 predicted.
Steroids and NAC monotherapy not indicated.
explanation.pearls: Definite UIP on HRCT with FVC 68 and DLCO 42 in a clinical IPF phenotype: refer to ILD MDT for pirfenidone or nintedanib; do not use steroids or NAC as primary therapy.

sources.label: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

options.rationale: Corticosteroid monotherapy does not benefit IPF and may harm; antifibrotic therapy is the standard. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

options.rationale: A definite UIP pattern on HRCT in a clinical context of IPF meets AU criteria to refer for antifibrotic therapy (pirfenidone or nintedanib) via a specialist ILD service. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

options.rationale: Definite UIP pattern on HRCT in the appropriate clinical context does not require surgical biopsy per current AU guidance; biopsy is reserved for probable or indeterminate UIP. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine monotherapy in IPF was not superior to placebo (PANTHER-IPF) and is not recommended. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

options.rationale: IPF is progressive; deferring antifibrotic therapy allows irreversible loss of function which cannot be recovered. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

explanation.summary: Australian severity-stratified community-acquired pneumonia (SMART-COP: Systolic BP under 90, Multilobar CXR, Albumin under 35, Respiratory rate raised, Tachycardia, Confusion, Oxygenation low, pH under 7.35) directs treatment intensity. SMART-COP 5 or above signals severe disease requiring ICU-capable care and dual IV antibiotic therapy: ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily (or benzylpenicillin) plus IV azithromycin 500 mg daily to cover Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypical pathogens (Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia). Moxifloxacin monotherapy is an alternative for beta-lactam allergy. Sepsis hour-1 bundle includes lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, IV antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate over 4 mmol/L, and vasopressor if not fluid-responsive.
key_points: SMART-COP 5+ triggers severe CAP pathway.
Severe CAP: IV ceftriaxone plus IV azithromycin.
Hour-1 sepsis bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluid.
Moxifloxacin monotherapy for severe beta-lactam allergy.
explanation.pearls: SMART-COP 5 with lactate 3.4 mandates IV ceftriaxone 1 g plus IV azithromycin 500 mg within the sepsis hour; cultures first, then antibiotics, then 30 mL/kg crystalloid.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

options.rationale: For severe CAP with SMART-COP 5 and organ dysfunction, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is the Australian eTG regimen rather than amoxicillin plus gentamicin. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

options.rationale: SMART-COP 5 mandates inpatient IV therapy with ICU review; oral outpatient treatment is unsafe. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

options.rationale: SMART-COP 5 defines severe CAP requiring ICU-capable care; the Australian eTG severe CAP regimen is IV ceftriaxone plus IV azithromycin (or moxifloxacin monotherapy if beta-lactam allergy). (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

options.rationale: Broad Gram negative and MRSA cover is not first-line for community-acquired pneumonia; ceftriaxone plus azithromycin covers typical and atypical pathogens. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

options.rationale: Meropenem is inappropriate first-line for CAP; it drives selection pressure for resistance and is reserved for hospital-acquired or resistant infection. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis in a non-pregnant adult who is systemically well and can tolerate oral fluids is managed as an outpatient per Australian eTG. First-line oral therapy is ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 7 days or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (double strength) BD for 14 days if fluoroquinolone contraindicated. Cefalexin 500 mg QID for 14 days is an alternative. Admission for IV therapy is required for severe sepsis, pregnancy, uncontrolled vomiting, urinary tract obstruction (needs urgent drainage), or failure of oral therapy at 48 hours. Urine culture guides definitive therapy; imaging (renal ultrasound or CT) is reserved for recurrent infection, poor response or suspected obstruction.
key_points: Uncomplicated pyelonephritis: oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 7 days.
Admission for IV: severe sepsis, pregnancy, vomiting, obstruction.
Trimethoprim short course is for cystitis only.
Nitrofurantoin does not treat pyelonephritis.
explanation.pearls: Well non-pregnant adult with pyelonephritis who tolerates oral fluids: outpatient ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 7 days with 48 hour review; admit if severe sepsis, pregnancy or ongoing vomiting.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection
Cochrane 2010: Antibiotic regimens for acute pyelonephritis

options.rationale: Trimethoprim short course treats uncomplicated cystitis not pyelonephritis; pyelonephritis requires an oral fluoroquinolone or cefalexin equivalent for 10 to 14 days. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection

options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate renal parenchymal concentrations for pyelonephritis and is restricted to cystitis. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection

options.rationale: IV therapy is reserved for severe sepsis, pregnancy, inability to tolerate oral, or failure of oral therapy; she is systemically well and tolerating fluids. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection

options.rationale: Uncomplicated pyelonephritis in a systemically well adult who tolerates oral intake is managed as an outpatient with oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 7 days per Australian eTG. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection

options.rationale: Amoxicillin resistance rates in E coli exceed 50 percent and empirical amoxicillin monotherapy is inadequate for pyelonephritis. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection

explanation.summary: Warfarin-associated major bleeding, including any intracranial haemorrhage or life-threatening bleed at any INR, requires immediate reversal per Australian THANZ consensus. The standard combination is IV vitamin K 10 mg (works over 6-24 hours) plus prothrombinex 25-50 units/kg (works within minutes to hours). Vitamin K provides sustained reversal by allowing hepatic synthesis of clotting factors; prothrombinex provides immediate factor II, VII, IX, X replacement. FFP is used only if prothrombinex is unavailable, at 15 mL/kg. Recheck INR at 30 minutes and repeat prothrombinex if INR remains above 1.5. Blood pressure control (systolic under 140) reduces haematoma expansion in ICH.
key_points: Warfarin major bleed: IV vitamin K + prothrombinex.
Vitamin K sustains reversal; prothrombinex is immediate.
FFP is a backup only when prothrombinex unavailable.
Idarucizumab is for dabigatran, andexanet for FXa inhibitors.
explanation.pearls: Warfarin ICH with INR 3.8: IV vitamin K 10 mg + prothrombinex 50 units/kg immediately; check INR at 30 min and target under 1.5; drop systolic BP to under 140 to limit expansion.

options.rationale: rFVIIa is not routinely used for warfarin reversal; prothrombinex provides balanced factor replacement and is the AU standard. (Source: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus)
Oral vitamin K is too slow (24 to 48 hours to lower INR) for a life-threatening ICH; IV route and factor replacement are required. (Source: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus)
FFP alone requires large volumes and delivers unpredictable factor levels; prothrombinex is preferred and provides faster INR correction. (Source: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus)
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, not warfarin; there is no role in warfarin-associated bleeding. (Source: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus)

Major bleeding on warfarin (any life-threatening or intracranial bleed) requires immediate reversal with IV vitamin K plus prothrombinex per Australian THANZ/AHRTC guidance; FFP alone is inadequate. (Source: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus)

explanation.summary: Australian HIV opportunistic infection prophylaxis follows CD4-based thresholds. Below 200 cells/microL: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg daily (or three times weekly) for Pneumocystis pneumonia; dapsone 100 mg daily is an alternative in sulfa allergy. Below 100 cells/microL with positive toxoplasma IgG: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole also covers toxoplasmosis (dapsone plus pyrimethamine-folinic acid in sulfa allergy). Below 50 cells/microL: MAC prophylaxis with azithromycin 1200 mg weekly, though it is being de-emphasised as early ART restores immunity rapidly. Prophylaxis is stopped once CD4 rises above 200 for at least 3 months on sustained virological suppression.
key_points: PCP prophylaxis starts at CD4 below 200 with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
Toxoplasma cover comes with the same drug when IgG is positive.
MAC prophylaxis is reserved for CD4 below 50 and is being de-emphasised.
Stop prophylaxis when CD4 above 200 for 3 months on suppressive ART.
explanation.pearls: At CD4 140 with negative toxoplasma IgG, start trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg daily for Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis; add MAC prophylaxis only if CD4 falls below 50.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - HIV opportunistic infections

options.rationale: Primary antifungal prophylaxis is not routine in Australian HIV care regardless of CD4 count at this level. (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Consensus)
CMV prophylaxis is not recommended primarily; treatment is initiated only if end-organ disease is diagnosed. (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Consensus)

Dapsone is an alternative to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in sulfa allergy; combined pyrimethamine-folinic acid is for toxoplasmosis in seropositive patients only. (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Consensus)

ASHM guidance starts trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim) at CD4 below 200 for Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis; toxoplasmosis prophylaxis is not required as IgG is negative. (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Consensus)
MAC prophylaxis is only added when CD4 falls below 50 in Australian guidance and is being de-emphasised with early ART. (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Consensus)

explanation.summary: The RACGP osteoporosis guideline uses DXA T-score, minimal trauma fracture history and 10-year absolute fracture risk (FRAX or Garvan) to decide pharmacotherapy. Pharmacotherapy is indicated for T-score at or below -2.5, or any minimal trauma vertebral fracture, or 10-year major osteoporotic fracture risk of 20 percent or more with any low bone density, or a hip fracture 3 percent or more. First-line agents are oral alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly. IV zoledronic acid 5 mg annually is an alternative for oral intolerance. Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneous 6 monthly is second-line, and abrupt cessation risks rebound vertebral fracture, so it needs a bisphosphonate follow-on if discontinued.
key_points: Pharmacotherapy is indicated for T-score at or below -2.5 or any minimal trauma vertebral fracture.
First-line is oral alendronate or risedronate weekly.
IV zoledronic acid annually is an alternative for oral intolerance.
Denosumab needs bisphosphonate follow-on if stopped to avoid rebound fracture.
explanation.pearls: A T-score of -2.5 or lower on DXA meets the RACGP threshold for pharmacotherapy; start alendronate 70 mg weekly with continued calcium and vitamin D.

sources.label: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.rationale: A T-score of -2.5 or lower meets the diagnostic criterion for osteoporosis; observation without pharmacotherapy is undertreatment. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.rationale: Teriparatide is reserved for severe osteoporosis with T-score below -3.0 and prior fracture on bisphosphonate; bisphosphonate is first-line here. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.rationale: Tibolone is not first-line osteoporosis therapy for a 66-year-old without vasomotor symptoms; bisphosphonate is preferred. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.rationale: Strontium ranelate carries cardiovascular risk and is now rarely used; bisphosphonates are the standard of care. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.rationale: RACGP osteoporosis guidelines recommend pharmacotherapy for T-score at or below -2.5 or any minimal trauma fracture; alendronate weekly is the first-line bisphosphonate. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency requires end-organ damage (encephalopathy, pulmonary oedema, acute kidney injury, aortic dissection, retinopathy grade 3-4) alongside severely elevated BP (generally above 180/120). Treatment uses IV antihypertensive therapy to reduce mean arterial pressure by approximately 25 percent over the first hour, then to 160/100-110 over the next 2 to 6 hours, then to normal over 24 to 48 hours. First-line agents include IV labetalol, IV GTN (if myocardial ischaemia or pulmonary oedema), IV hydralazine, or IV clevidipine. Nitroprusside is reserved for refractory cases due to cyanide toxicity risk. Aortic dissection requires more rapid BP and heart rate control (SBP below 120, HR below 60) with esmolol plus GTN or nitroprusside.
key_points: Hypertensive emergency needs end-organ damage plus severe BP.
Target 25 percent MAP reduction in the first hour.
First-line agents: IV labetalol, IV GTN, IV hydralazine or IV clevidipine.
Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated due to uncontrolled drops.
explanation.pearls: Reduce MAP by no more than 25 percent in the first hour in hypertensive emergency with IV labetalol or GTN; sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated.

sources.label: NHMRC Guide to management of hypertension

options.rationale: Australian and international guidance treats hypertensive emergency with 25 percent MAP reduction in the first hour using IV labetalol or GTN; overly aggressive reduction risks watershed cerebral ischaemia. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)
Rapid BP normalisation risks cerebral, coronary and renal hypoperfusion; the target is 25 percent MAP reduction in the first hour. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)
Sublingual nifedipine causes uncontrolled precipitous BP drops and is not recommended in hypertensive emergency. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)
Oral ramipril is too slow-acting for hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage; IV therapy is required for controlled reduction. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)
Furosemide addresses volume overload and pulmonary oedema but is not first-line for hypertensive emergency without those features. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency where diagnosis rests on clinical signs (pain out of proportion, rapid progression, crepitus, dusky skin, sensory changes over the affected area, systemic sepsis) supplemented by the Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotising Fasciitis (LRINEC) score: CRP, WCC, Hb, sodium, creatinine, glucose. A score of 6 or more raises suspicion; a score of 8 or more is high probability. However, LRINEC does not replace clinical judgement and imaging must not delay surgery when suspicion is high. Empirical antibiotics are broad-spectrum: piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin (for toxin suppression). Urgent surgical debridement is the definitive intervention; delay increases mortality substantially.
key_points: Necrotising fasciitis diagnosis is largely clinical; imaging should not delay surgery.
LRINEC score aids risk stratification but does not replace clinical judgement.
Empirical antibiotics: meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin plus clindamycin.
Urgent surgical debridement is the definitive intervention.
explanation.pearls: In suspected necrotising fasciitis, pain out of proportion plus crepitus plus sepsis in a diabetic mandates immediate surgical review and IV meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin before any imaging.

options.rationale: Oral therapy is inadequate for necrotising fasciitis; parenteral broad-spectrum cover and urgent surgery are required. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

Pain out of proportion, crepitus, systemic sepsis and LRINEC-score risk factors in a diabetic mandates urgent surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin for toxin suppression. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

Necrotising fasciitis needs both broad-spectrum antibiotics with anaerobic and toxin-suppression cover plus urgent surgical debridement; monotherapy misses gram-negative and anaerobic pathogens. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

MRI delays definitive surgery and should not precede operative exploration when the clinical suspicion is strong; the diagnosis is clinical or surgical. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)
Hyperbaric oxygen may be adjunctive later but is never a substitute for surgical debridement and antibiotics in the acute presentation. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency in primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency, typically precipitated by illness, missed doses, surgery, trauma or emotional stress. Recognition rests on the combination of shock (relative hypotension, tachycardia), electrolyte disturbance (hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia in primary), hypoglycaemia, and often reduced conscious state. Immediate management is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg over 24 hours by continuous infusion (or 50 mg six-hourly IV or IM), rapid IV crystalloid to correct volume and sodium deficit, and glucose replacement. At these doses hydrocortisone provides mineralocorticoid effect so separate fludrocortisone is not needed acutely. Precipitating illness must be treated concurrently.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours infusion is standard.
Aggressive fluid and glucose correction alongside steroid replacement.
Fludrocortisone not needed acutely at these hydrocortisone doses.
Sick day rules and emergency IM hydrocortisone at home prevent recurrence.
explanation.pearls: In adrenal crisis give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus and 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion with IV fluid and glucose; no separate fludrocortisone needed acutely.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Australia adrenal insufficiency guidance

options.rationale: Oral therapy is not reliable in a vomiting hypotensive patient; parenteral hydrocortisone is required. (Source: Endocrine Society Australia adrenal insufficiency guidance)

explanation.summary: Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) is an immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy typically triggered by preceding infection (Campylobacter jejuni, CMV, EBV, Zika, Mycoplasma) 1 to 4 weeks earlier. Diagnosis rests on progressive weakness plus areflexia, supported by albuminocytological dissociation on CSF (raised protein with normal cell count) and nerve conduction studies showing demyelination. Prognostic markers for respiratory failure include rapid progression, bulbar weakness, autonomic instability and FVC below 20 mL/kg (or 1 L in an average adult). Treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg divided over 5 days OR plasma exchange (5 sessions over 2 weeks); the two are equally effective but not combined. Corticosteroids are ineffective and not used.
key_points: IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days is first-line; plasma exchange is equally effective.
Corticosteroids are ineffective in GBS.
FVC below 20 mL/kg or 1 L predicts need for ventilation.
Erasmus GBS Respiratory Insufficiency Score aids risk stratification.
explanation.pearls: In GBS with rapidly progressive weakness and FVC 1.6 L, start IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days and admit for respiratory monitoring; steroids do not help.

options.rationale: Oral corticosteroids are not evidence-based for GBS and delay definitive treatment. (Source: RACP Guillain-Barre syndrome resources)
Rituximab is not indicated for acute GBS; IVIG or plasma exchange is the standard. (Source: RACP Guillain-Barre syndrome resources)
Progressive weakness with FVC below 20 mL/kg requires immunotherapy to shorten hospital stay and reduce ventilation risk. (Source: RACP Guillain-Barre syndrome resources)

explanation.summary: Differentiating shock subtypes is essential in the deteriorating ICU patient. Septic shock characteristically features warm peripheries early, low SVR, high or normal cardiac output, and a collapsible IVC after fluid resuscitation. Cardiogenic shock features cool peripheries, high SVR (often reflected clinically in peripheral shutdown), reduced cardiac output, raised JVP, pulmonary crackles, plethoric IVC and evidence of pump failure on echocardiography. The clue in this case is the emergence of ECG ischaemic changes, rising troponin, new LV dysfunction on echo and IVC plethora, in a patient already on high-dose noradrenaline. This suggests demand ischaemia (type 2 MI) or superimposed acute cardiomyopathy driven by sepsis (septic cardiomyopathy or takotsubo).
key_points: Plethoric IVC with pulmonary crackles argues against fluid-responsive septic shock alone.
Rising troponin and new ECG changes suggest superimposed cardiogenic component.
Inotropic support (dobutamine or adrenaline) addresses the pump failure.
Further fluid worsens pulmonary oedema in cardiogenic shock.
explanation.pearls: In septic shock with rising troponin, new LV dysfunction and IVC plethora, switch strategy from further fluid to inotropic support with dobutamine and urgent cardiology input for mechanical support consideration.

options.rationale: Additional fluid in the presence of raised JVP, crackles and plethoric IVC will worsen pulmonary oedema and cardiac strain. (Source: Australian eTG: Critical care - Shock)
Vasopressin has a role as second-line vasopressor in septic shock but does not address the cardiogenic component driving the deterioration. (Source: Australian eTG: Critical care - Shock)
Bolus vasopressor use is a temporising measure in the ward setting; noradrenaline infusion is preferred in septic and mixed shock. (Source: Australian eTG: Critical care - Shock)
Diuresis in a patient with cardiogenic shock and a rising lactate risks worsening hypotension; inotropic support must come first. (Source: Australian eTG: Critical care - Shock)

New troponin rise, ECG changes, reduced EF and IVC plethora indicate superimposed cardiogenic shock; further fluids worsen pulmonary oedema, while inotropes and cardiology input address the LV dysfunction. (Source: Australian eTG: Critical care - Shock; RACP Cardiology guidance)

explanation.summary: Infective endocarditis is diagnosed by the modified Duke criteria: definite endocarditis requires 2 major, or 1 major and 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria. Major criteria are typical organisms in 2 separate blood cultures plus evidence of endocardial involvement on imaging (vegetation, abscess, new regurgitation, prosthetic dehiscence). Native valve viridans streptococcal endocarditis is treated with 4 weeks of penicillin or ceftriaxone, or 2 weeks combined with gentamicin. Prosthetic valve viridans streptococcal endocarditis is treated with 6 weeks of penicillin plus 2 weeks of gentamicin; surgery is indicated for heart failure, uncontrolled infection, large vegetation, abscess or prosthetic dehiscence.
key_points: Two positive blood cultures with typical organism plus echo evidence = definite endocarditis.
Prosthetic viridans strep endocarditis: penicillin 6 weeks plus gentamicin 2 weeks.
Native viridans strep endocarditis: penicillin 4 weeks or penicillin plus gentamicin 2 weeks.
Surgical indications include heart failure, uncontrolled infection, large vegetation, abscess.
explanation.pearls: Prosthetic valve viridans streptococcal endocarditis in Australia is treated with 6 weeks of intravenous benzylpenicillin plus synergistic gentamicin for the first 2 weeks.

options.rationale: Prosthetic valve endocarditis requires prolonged intravenous therapy; oral is not appropriate for empirical treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective Endocarditis)

Prosthetic valve viridans strep endocarditis requires combination therapy with an aminoglycoside and gentamicin for the first 2 weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective Endocarditis)

Vancomycin plus rifampicin is used for Staphylococcus aureus prosthetic valve endocarditis with penicillin allergy; not first-line for viridans strep. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective Endocarditis)

Viridans streptococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis is treated with 6 weeks of penicillin plus 2 weeks of synergistic gentamicin per Therapeutic Guidelines. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective Endocarditis)
Flucloxacillin covers staphylococci and is not the drug of choice for viridans streptococcal endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective Endocarditis)

explanation.summary: Screening for latent tuberculosis is required before starting biologic therapy or other significant immunosuppression, because reactivation carries high morbidity. Screening involves symptom review, chest radiograph and either tuberculin skin test or an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA); IGRAs are preferred in BCG-vaccinated individuals as they are not affected by prior vaccination. Positive screening with negative active-disease workup indicates latent tuberculosis. Standard treatment options are 9 months of isoniazid plus pyridoxine, 4 months of rifampicin, or 3-4 months of combined rifampicin plus isoniazid; biologic therapy can begin after at least 4 weeks of LTBI treatment.
key_points: IGRAs are unaffected by BCG vaccination unlike tuberculin skin testing.
Positive IGRA plus negative active-disease workup indicates latent tuberculosis.
Standard LTBI treatment: 9 months isoniazid plus pyridoxine.
Biologic can begin after at least 4 weeks of LTBI treatment.
explanation.pearls: Before TNF-alpha inhibitor start in a BCG-vaccinated patient, a positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus with clear CXR is latent TB; treat with 9 months of isoniazid plus pyridoxine.

explanation.summary: The sepsis hour-1 bundle is: measure lactate, obtain blood cultures, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics, begin 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate 4 mmol/L or higher, and start vasopressors during or after fluid resuscitation to maintain MAP 65 mmHg or higher. Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor, with vasopressin added second-line to reduce noradrenaline dose and adrenaline reserved for refractory shock. Hydrocortisone 200 mg daily is added for shock refractory to fluid and vasopressor. Source control and lactate clearance monitoring guide ongoing management.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, 30 mL/kg fluid, vasopressor if needed.
Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor targeting MAP 65 mmHg or higher.
Vasopressin added second-line; adrenaline for refractory shock.
Hydrocortisone added for refractory shock on ongoing vasopressor.
explanation.pearls: In septic shock with persistent hypotension after 30 mL/kg crystalloid, start noradrenaline first-line targeting mean arterial pressure at or above 65 mmHg.

options.rationale: Persistent hypotension and rising lactate after 30 mL/kg of crystalloid meet septic shock criteria; noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor targeting MAP 65 or above per the Surviving Sepsis and ANZICS guidance. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Guidance)
Continued aggressive fluid loading after 30 mL/kg with persistent hypotension risks pulmonary oedema; vasopressor is the appropriate escalation. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Guidance)
Hydrocortisone in septic shock is used in refractory shock requiring ongoing vasopressor; it is not a first-line replacement for vasopressor. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Guidance)
The clinical picture is septic shock from likely pneumonia; delaying vasopressor for imaging is inappropriate at this stage of resuscitation. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Guidance)
Adrenaline is a second-line agent for septic shock; noradrenaline is first-line based on lower arrhythmogenicity. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Guidance)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency with mortality of around 20-30 percent even with treatment. Discriminators from cellulitis include pain out of proportion to skin findings, rapid progression, systemic toxicity, dusky discolouration, bullae, subcutaneous crepitus (less than 40 percent of cases) and firm woody induration; absence of gas on plain radiograph does not exclude it. The LRINEC score (CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, glucose) 6 or above suggests intermediate risk and 8 or above high risk. Management is urgent surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin), with clindamycin included specifically to suppress exotoxin production.
key_points: Pain out of proportion, dusky skin, bullae, systemic toxicity suggest necrotising fasciitis.
LRINEC score of 6+ intermediate risk, 8+ high risk.
Absence of tissue gas does not exclude the diagnosis.
Urgent surgical debridement plus piperacillin-tazobactam, clindamycin, vancomycin.
explanation.pearls: In a septic patient with pain out of proportion, dusky skin and LRINEC 6 or above, arrange urgent surgical debridement with piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin; imaging must not delay theatre.

explanation.summary: The Endocrine Society recommends three first-line screening tests for Cushing syndrome, with two abnormal results required for diagnosis: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (cortisol under 50 nmol/L is a normal response), late-night salivary cortisol on two occasions, and 24-hour urinary free cortisol on two occasions. Exclude exogenous glucocorticoid use first. After biochemical confirmation, plasma ACTH determines whether the process is ACTH-dependent (pituitary adenoma commonest, followed by ectopic ACTH) or ACTH-independent (adrenal adenoma, adrenal carcinoma). Further tests including high-dose dexamethasone, corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) stimulation, and inferior petrosal sinus sampling then localise the source. Imaging is guided by biochemistry.
key_points: First-line screening: 1 mg overnight DST OR late-night salivary cortisol OR 24 h urinary free cortisol.
Two abnormal screening tests are required for diagnosis.
Plasma ACTH then distinguishes ACTH-dependent from independent disease.
Imaging follows biochemical confirmation, not before.
explanation.pearls: First-line Cushing syndrome screening uses the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (positive if morning cortisol above 50 nmol/L), the late-night salivary cortisol, or the 24-hour urinary free cortisol.

options.rationale: ACTH measurement is used AFTER Cushing syndrome is confirmed to establish the source; it is not a first-line screening test. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

High-dose dexamethasone suppression is used AFTER confirmed Cushing syndrome to differentiate pituitary from ectopic ACTH source, not for screening. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

The 1 mg overnight DST is one of three Endocrine Society first-line screening tests (with 24 h urinary free cortisol and late night salivary cortisol); failure to suppress below 50 nmol/L is positive. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

Pituitary MRI is used after confirming ACTH-dependent Cushing; up to 10 percent of the general population have incidental pituitary lesions, and imaging pre-diagnosis leads to false-positive workup. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)
Phaeochromocytoma is a differential for episodic hypertension, not for Cushingoid features with muscle weakness and striae. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is life-threatening and demands treatment before biochemical confirmation. Patients on long-term supraphysiological glucocorticoid therapy (prednisolone 7.5 mg or higher daily for 3 weeks) suppress the HPA axis and require stress-dose steroid during intercurrent illness. Standard treatment is hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenous bolus, then 200 mg over 24 hours as 50 mg 6-hourly or continuous infusion, plus intravenous fluid resuscitation with saline and dextrose to correct hypovolaemia and hypoglycaemia. High-dose hydrocortisone provides adequate mineralocorticoid effect so fludrocortisone is not needed acutely; dexamethasone can be substituted only when a Synacthen test is planned within hours.
key_points: Long-term prednisolone 7.5 mg or more for 3+ weeks suppresses the HPA axis.
Treat adrenal crisis with 100 mg IV hydrocortisone before biochemical confirmation.
Follow with 200 mg over 24 hours plus glucose-saline resuscitation.
Fludrocortisone not needed acutely due to hydrocortisone's mineralocorticoid effect.
explanation.pearls: Adrenal crisis is treated with intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg over 24 hours plus glucose-saline resuscitation; do not wait for a Synacthen test.

options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is oral only and its mineralocorticoid effect is not required acutely because high-dose hydrocortisone at 100 mg or higher provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)

Adrenal crisis is life-threatening; treatment must not be delayed for diagnostic testing when clinical picture and low random cortisol strongly suggest crisis. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)

Oral prednisolone is unreliable in a vomiting, shocked patient and provides inadequate stress-dose steroid; parenteral hydrocortisone is required. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)

Adrenal crisis is treated with hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus followed by 200 mg over 24 hours plus intravenous glucose-saline for hypoglycaemia and hypovolaemia. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)

Dexamethasone provides glucocorticoid effect but no mineralocorticoid activity; hydrocortisone is preferred in acute adrenal crisis for its dual effect at 100 mg dose. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome causes: exogenous glucocorticoid (commonest overall), pituitary corticotroph adenoma (Cushing disease, commonest endogenous), ectopic ACTH secretion (small cell lung cancer, carcinoid), and primary adrenal disease (adenoma, carcinoma, bilateral hyperplasia). ACTH is elevated in ACTH-dependent causes and suppressed in ACTH-independent causes. High-dose dexamethasone suppression test discriminates: Cushing disease usually suppresses cortisol by 50 percent or more (adenoma retains partial feedback), whereas ectopic ACTH does not suppress. Ectopic ACTH from SCLC classically presents rapidly with severe hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (very high cortisol overwhelms 11-beta-HSD2, causing mineralocorticoid effect), hyperpigmentation (very high ACTH cross-reacts with MSH receptors), truncal wasting rather than classic Cushingoid habitus (rapid onset, cachexia), and hyperglycaemia. Management is directed at the underlying tumour plus cortisol-blocking agents like ketoconazole or metyrapone.
key_points: Elevated ACTH indicates ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome (pituitary or ectopic).
High-dose DST: Cushing disease suppresses >=50 percent; ectopic ACTH does not.
Ectopic ACTH from SCLC causes rapid onset, hypokalaemic alkalosis, hyperpigmentation.
Truncal wasting rather than classic Cushingoid habitus is typical of ectopic ACTH.
explanation.pearls: In hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with hyperpigmentation, failure to suppress on high-dose dexamethasone and a lung mass in a smoker, suspect ectopic ACTH from small cell lung carcinoma.

options.rationale: Cushing disease typically suppresses more than 50 percent on high-dose DST because the adenoma retains some feedback sensitivity; failure to suppress here argues against a pituitary source. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)
An adrenal source is ACTH-independent so ACTH would be suppressed, not elevated; the markedly elevated ACTH rules out adrenal adenoma. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)
Exogenous glucocorticoid suppresses endogenous ACTH; the very high ACTH here excludes this. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

Pituitary adenomas do not metastasise to the lung; the picture, especially failure to suppress and speed of onset, is not consistent with Cushing disease. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

Ectopic ACTH from SCLC classically presents with acute weight loss and truncal wasting (not obesity), profound hypokalaemic alkalosis, hyperpigmentation from very high ACTH and MSH, and failure to suppress on high-dose DST. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

explanation.summary: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis in HIV is CD4-count driven. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg daily (or 3 times weekly) starts at CD4 below 200 cells/microL, or with a history of AIDS-defining illness, and continues until CD4 is above 200 for at least 3 months on suppressive ART. This regimen also covers Toxoplasma reactivation, which is the concern above CD4 100 in Toxoplasma-IgG-positive patients. Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis is no longer routinely recommended if effective ART is being started. Primary cryptococcal, fungal or herpes virus prophylaxis is not routine. Latent TB treatment follows a positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold or Mantoux; a positive screen prompts a 4-month rifampicin or 9-month isoniazid course.
key_points: PCP prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole at CD4 below 200.
Same regimen covers Toxoplasma reactivation in IgG-positive patients.
MAC prophylaxis no longer routine on modern ART.
Latent TB treatment only for QuantiFERON-positive patients.
explanation.pearls: Any patient with HIV and CD4 below 200 cells/microL starts trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg daily for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and Toxoplasma cover.

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection is diagnosed by a positive interferon-gamma release assay (QuantiFERON-TB Gold or T-SPOT.TB) or a positive tuberculin skin test with a compatible risk profile, in the absence of clinical or radiological evidence of active disease. QuantiFERON does not cross-react with BCG or with most non-tuberculous mycobacteria. In Australia, NTAC offers treatment where the benefit outweighs the risk; healthcare workers, migrants from high-burden countries in the last 5 years, HIV, TNF-alpha inhibitor candidates and paediatric contacts are priority groups. Preferred regimens are 4 months of rifampicin (4R), 3 months of rifampicin plus isoniazid (3HR) or 3 months of once-weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine (3HP), all shorter and better tolerated than the traditional 9 months of isoniazid. Monthly clinical and LFT monitoring is standard. Baseline hepatitis B and C serology and pregnancy status are checked before starting.
key_points: QuantiFERON does not cross-react with BCG.
Latent TB treatment preferred: 4R, 3HR or 3HP over 9H.
Monthly clinical and LFT monitoring during treatment.
Sputum only if active TB suspected on symptoms or imaging.
explanation.pearls: For latent TB in a healthy adult, offer 4 months of rifampicin (4R) with monthly LFT monitoring; 9 months of isoniazid is now second choice due to hepatotoxicity and adherence.

explanation.summary: The Australian Sepsis Kills and Surviving Sepsis campaign Hour-1 bundle applies to any adult with suspected sepsis and hypotension or lactate above 2 mmol/L. It comprises: measure serum lactate; obtain blood cultures (before antibiotics if possible without delay); administer broad-spectrum antibiotics within an hour; give 30 mL/kg intravenous crystalloid within 3 hours (aim for early completion) for hypotension or lactate at or above 4 mmol/L; and start vasopressors (usually noradrenaline) to keep mean arterial pressure at least 65 mmHg if fluids do not restore perfusion. Empirical antibiotic depends on source: ceftriaxone 2 g IV for community-acquired urosepsis or CAP, piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin for hospital-acquired or neutropenic sepsis. Repeat lactate at the end of hour 1 guides fluid and vasopressor titration. Source control (e.g. drainage of an obstructed kidney) is arranged as soon as safely possible.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: cultures, lactate, antibiotics, 30 mL/kg fluid, vasopressor if needed.
Ceftriaxone 2 g IV first-line for AU community-acquired urosepsis.
Give 30 mL/kg crystalloid within the first hour for hypotension or lactate over 4.
Repeat lactate to titrate resuscitation.
explanation.pearls: For adult community-acquired urosepsis, the Hour-1 bundle is lactate, cultures, IV ceftriaxone 2 g, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, then repeat lactate to guide vasopressor start.

explanation.summary: Addisonian (adrenal) crisis presents as hypotension, hypovolaemia, altered consciousness, gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia in a patient with primary adrenal insufficiency. Typical triggers are intercurrent illness with vomiting, missed steroid doses, or a stressor without stress-dose adjustment. Empirical IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately (then 50 mg every 6 hours or a 200 mg per 24-hour infusion) is the priority, with 1 litre 0.9 percent normal saline (with 5 percent dextrose if hypoglycaemic) in the first hour and further crystalloid guided by response. Hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia typically correct with steroid and fluid; specific therapy for either is rarely needed. Once oral tolerance returns, transition to double-dose oral hydrocortisone tapering over a few days back to baseline. Sick-day education (double-dose oral for illness; parenteral hydrocortisone kit at home) prevents recurrence.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately; do not wait for ACTH stimulation.
1 litre normal saline (with dextrose if hypoglycaemic) in the first hour.
Sodium and potassium usually correct with steroid and fluid alone.
Sick-day plan and home parenteral kit prevent recurrence.
explanation.pearls: For a known Addisonian in shock with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia, give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg and 1 litre normal saline with 5 percent dextrose in the first hour.

options.rationale: Addisonian crisis with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia demands empirical IV hydrocortisone 100 mg without waiting for ACTH stimulation, plus saline with dextrose for volume and glucose. (Source: ESA Consensus Statement on Adrenal Insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection is classified by the Stanford system as Type A (involving the ascending aorta) or Type B (distal to the left subclavian). Type A is a surgical emergency requiring urgent cardiothoracic repair; Type B is usually medically managed unless complicated by malperfusion, rupture or refractory pain. Medical management focuses on reducing aortic wall shear stress: heart rate is targeted first with intravenous beta blockade (esmolol or labetalol) to 60 to 80/min, then blood pressure with a vasodilator (glyceryl trinitrate or sodium nitroprusside) to a systolic 100 to 120 mmHg. Vasodilators without prior beta blockade cause reflex tachycardia and increase shear stress. Anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy are contraindicated. Analgesia with intravenous opioid is important. Retrieval to a cardiothoracic centre is prioritised for Type A dissection.
key_points: Heart rate control with beta blocker before vasodilator in dissection.
Target heart rate 60 to 80/min, systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg.
Anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy are contraindicated.
Type A dissection is a surgical emergency requiring urgent repair.
explanation.pearls: For acute Type A aortic dissection, start IV esmolol to target heart rate 60 to 80/min, then IV glyceryl trinitrate to systolic 100 to 120 mmHg; never vasodilate before rate control.

options.rationale: Vasodilator without prior beta blockade causes reflex tachycardia that increases aortic shear stress and worsens the dissection; heart rate control precedes blood pressure reduction. (Source: RACP Aortic Dissection Consensus)

Anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy are contraindicated in acute aortic dissection because they worsen bleeding into the false lumen and pericardium. (Source: RACP Aortic Dissection Consensus)
Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia and increases aortic shear stress; a beta blocker must be used first for rate control. (Source: RACP Aortic Dissection Consensus)

Analgesia is important but does not address the ongoing aortic shear stress driving dissection propagation; rate and BP control are the immediate priorities. (Source: RACP Aortic Dissection Consensus)

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension (usually diastolic above 120 mmHg or systolic above 180 mmHg) with acute end-organ damage: encephalopathy, papilloedema, acute kidney injury, pulmonary oedema, myocardial ischaemia or acute aortic syndrome. Treatment is parenteral titratable therapy in a monitored setting, with a staged reduction: mean arterial pressure by no more than 25 percent in the first hour, then to 160/100 mmHg over the next 2 to 6 hours, and to near baseline over 24 to 48 hours. Faster reduction risks cerebral, renal or coronary watershed injury. Choice of agent depends on the target organ: labetalol or nicardipine for encephalopathy or renal failure; glyceryl trinitrate for pulmonary oedema or acute coronary syndrome; hydralazine and labetalol for pre-eclampsia. Sublingual nifedipine is unsafe due to uncontrolled precipitous drops. Investigate for a secondary cause once BP is controlled.
key_points: Emergency = severe hypertension plus acute end-organ damage.
Reduce MAP by no more than 25 percent in the first hour.
Labetalol or nicardipine for encephalopathy; nitrate for pulmonary oedema.
Sublingual short-acting nifedipine is unsafe.
explanation.pearls: In hypertensive emergency with encephalopathy, use IV labetalol 20 to 80 mg boluses to reduce mean arterial pressure by no more than 25 percent in the first hour.

options.rationale: Oral therapy is too slow and unreliable in a hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage; IV therapy titratable in a monitored setting is required. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)

Sublingual short-acting nifedipine causes precipitous uncontrolled drops in BP and risks stroke; it is not recommended for hypertensive emergency. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)

AU hypertensive emergency management is IV labetalol (or glyceryl trinitrate) with staged reduction of MAP by no more than 25 percent in the first hour to prevent watershed injury. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)

Oral therapy is inadequate for hypertensive emergency with encephalopathy; parenteral titratable therapy is required and simply restarting missed medications is unsafe. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)

explanation.summary: Diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome follows a two-step approach: confirm autonomous cortisol excess, then identify the source. First-line screening tests are 24-hour urinary free cortisol on 2 separate collections, late-night salivary cortisol on 2 different nights, and 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test; two abnormal tests confirm the diagnosis. Once confirmed, plasma ACTH divides into ACTH-independent (ACTH suppressed, source is adrenal) and ACTH-dependent (ACTH detectable or elevated, source is pituitary or ectopic). For ACTH-dependent Cushing's, a high-dose 8 mg overnight DST with pituitary MRI is next; suppression at high dose plus a pituitary lesion supports Cushing's disease. Non-suppression, no visible pituitary lesion, or discordance prompts inferior petrosal sinus sampling. Ectopic ACTH sources (bronchial carcinoid, small cell lung cancer, medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma) usually do not suppress at high dose. Confounders for the low-dose DST include night-shift work, oestrogens, and CYP450-inducing drugs.
key_points: Two abnormal first-line tests confirm Cushing's biochemically.
ACTH divides into independent (adrenal) and dependent (pituitary or ectopic).
High-dose DST plus pituitary MRI localise ACTH-dependent Cushing's.
Ectopic ACTH usually does not suppress at high dose.
explanation.pearls: After confirming Cushing's biochemically with two positive first-line tests and a non-suppressed ACTH, proceed to a high-dose 8 mg dexamethasone suppression test with pituitary MRI to distinguish pituitary from ectopic source.

options.rationale: Three separate first-line tests are positive with clinical features and morbidity; delay for repeat testing is unsafe and the shift-work confounder does not explain all three abnormal tests. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline)

Medical adrenolysis is a temporising measure before surgery, not a diagnostic step; localisation of the ACTH source is required. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline)

explanation.summary: Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) is an acute inflammatory polyneuropathy typically preceded by Campylobacter, CMV, EBV or Mycoplasma infection, with ascending symmetric weakness, areflexia, autonomic dysfunction and eventual respiratory involvement. Miller Fisher syndrome (MFS) is a variant defined by ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia (anti-GQ1b antibody positive in over 90 percent), and overlap syndromes are common. Diagnosis relies on the clinical picture plus CSF albuminocytological dissociation (raised protein, normal cell count, may be normal in the first week) and demyelinating pattern on nerve conduction studies. Treatment is IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days or plasma exchange (5 sessions over 2 weeks) - the two are equally effective, and steroids do not help. Respiratory monitoring with 4-hourly FVC is critical: FVC below 20 mL/kg, negative inspiratory force below -30 cmH2O or bulbar dysfunction prompts HDU/ICU admission and consideration of intubation.
key_points: Miller Fisher triad: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia (anti-GQ1b positive).
CSF albuminocytological dissociation supports GBS spectrum.
IVIG or plasma exchange are equally effective; steroids do not help.
Monitor FVC 4-hourly; intubate for FVC below 20 mL/kg or bulbar failure.
explanation.pearls: For Miller Fisher-Guillain-Barre overlap, give IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days and monitor FVC 4-hourly; intubate for FVC below 20 mL/kg or bulbar failure.

options.rationale: Steroids do not help Guillain-Barre or its variants and are potentially harmful; the CSF albuminocytological dissociation and reflex loss with recent Campylobacter-like illness point to Miller Fisher-Guillain-Barre overlap. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)
Areflexia and CSF albuminocytological dissociation are not features of myasthenia; edrophonium (Tensilon) is not appropriate here. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)

MRI brainstem is normal and CSF pleocytosis is absent; HSV encephalitis does not fit and IV aciclovir does not treat Guillain-Barre or Miller Fisher. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)

CSF shows albuminocytological dissociation without pleocytosis; bacterial meningitis is unlikely and neither antibiotic nor steroid treats Miller Fisher. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)

The clinical picture (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia with limb weakness) plus CSF albuminocytological dissociation is Miller Fisher-Guillain-Barre overlap; IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days plus respiratory monitoring is standard AU therapy. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)
